ratings.plot: The eldest daughter of a broken and troubled family works to keep the family together and look after her younger siblings, who are slipping into a life of crime.

verdict.reason: A rare New York screening of Hou Hsiao-hsien's essential work on family dissolution and urban struggle. The DCP restoration at Metrograph is the only way to see this 1987 masterpiece theatrically right now.

ratings.plot: All the while, Master Chu tries to find his place in the foreign American world.

verdict.reason: Ang Lee's directorial debut deserves a big screen revival at one of the city's best venues. The film's precise balance of humor and tenderness in a cross-cultural family clash plays better theatrically than anywhere else.

ratings.plot: Within the urban gloom of Taipei, four youths face alienation, loneliness, and moments of existential crisis amidst a series of minor crimes.

verdict.reason: Tsai Ming-liang's debut is essential Taiwan cinema and a rare theatrical showing at Metrograph does not come often. Urban alienation has never looked this hypnotic or felt this true.

ratings.plot: Things go wrong for a high ranking mobster when he doesn't follow his boss's orders.

verdict.reason: Kim Jee-woon's most controlled work—a revenge thriller that earns its violence through precision and moral weight. Metrograph's DCP print gives the compositional brutality the clarity it deserves.

ratings.plot: Based on a true story, primarily on a conflict between two youth gangs, a 14-year-old boy's girlfriend conflicts with the head of one gang for an unclear reason, until finally the conflict comes to a violent climax.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip if you can commit to four hours of Edward Yang's masterwork on the big screen. Metrograph is showing a restored DCP of one of cinema's greatest examinations of adolescent violence and moral drift.

ratings.plot: In Mumbai, Nurse Prabha's routine is troubled when she receives an unexpected gift from her estranged husband. Her younger roommate, Anu, tries in vain to find a spot in the city to be intimate with her boyfriend.

verdict.reason: A rare film about interior lives and quiet longing that justifies the theatrical commitment. Kapadia's visual control—the city becomes a character of confinement and possibility—demands the scale and image quality a theater provides.

ratings.plot: A young couple leave their mining town home for Taipei where they struggle to eke out a living in an industrial wasteland.

verdict.reason: Hou Hsiao-Hsien's Taipei industrial romance is a masterpiece of patient visual storytelling and the Metrograph DCP restoration makes this the only way to see it. A 1986 film that moves like air and feels like memory.

ratings.plot: Ryuichi Sakamoto's last performance, a concert film featuring just him and his piano playing for the last time before passing away.

verdict.reason: A final document of one of music's great minds at the piano—this is not a concert film you can replace with a recording. Neo Sora captures something sacred in the space between Sakamoto and his instrument that demands the theater's acoustic presence.

ratings.plot: K2's first winter ascent claimed 5 lives, revealing modern alpinism's struggles with commercialization, social media impact, and conflicts between marginalized climbers and traditional elites.

verdict.reason: Amir Bar-Lev's documentary about K2's first winter ascent is essential viewing on the specific stakes of modern mountaineering. The film captures a real tragedy that exposes class fracture and commercial pressure in extreme sport, best witnessed in a theater where the altitude and moral weight can breathe.

ratings.plot: A handsome prince rides a flying horse to faraway lands and embarks on magical adventures, which include befriending a witch, meeting Aladdin, battling demons and falling in love with a princess.

verdict.reason: The oldest surviving narrative feature film and a silent masterpiece of silhouette animation—see it on the big screen at Film Forum where the delicate cutout artistry registers as intended. Reiniger's intricate frame-by-frame craftsmanship and fluid character movement hold up because the aesthetic was never about technical flash, just pure visual storytelling.

ratings.plot: When three American doctors-Palestinian, Jewish, and Zoroastrian-enter Gaza to save lives, they find themselves caught between medicine and politics, risking everything to expose the truth.

verdict.reason: A documentary about three doctors working across religious divides in Gaza demands to be seen while the crisis unfolds and the film is in theaters. Poh Si Teng brings journalists' discipline to a story where medicine and witness-bearing become the same act.

ratings.plot: Misael lives as an independent logger in the woods, enjoying his solitary freedom. When he must care for his older sister, his peaceful existence is upended and the foundations of his carefully constructed life begin to fall apart.

verdict.reason: Lisandro Alonso's new film arrives at Lincoln Center, where a maestro of deliberate landscape cinema deserves a theater and a patient audience. The collision between solitude and obligation—shot in Alonso's glacial, observational style—is the kind of quiet structural work that demands the size and silence of a cinema.

ratings.plot: A glimpse at the lives of two petty criminals in Taipei.

verdict.reason: A rare New York showing of Hou Hsiao-hsien's masterwork on 35mm at Lincoln Center—this is the kind of screening you don't get twice. The camera holds still while Taipei's underworld moves through the frame with the precision of a poet's line break.

ratings.plot: A group of high school students sets off on a school trip to discover the ruins of Pompeii. They are seized by a sense of vertigo. They allow themselves to be overwhelmed by desire and anger, until they surrender completely.

verdict.reason: A rare film about teenage intoxication and desire shot with real formal ambition at one of New York's premier venues. Atlan uses Pompeii's stasis to frame how adolescent bodies move through space and surrender to impulse, and the 16mm cinematography catches light the way memory does.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem

ratings.plot: A decade post-death, filmmaker William Greaves reveals his final work: footage of a 1972 gathering he arranged with Harlem Renaissance legends, which he deemed his most significant capture.

verdict.reason: A posthumous William Greaves film showing archival footage of Harlem Renaissance figures from 1972 is a rare historical document that belongs on the big screen. Lincoln Center is the only venue, and this is the kind of cinema history that dissolves into the ether if you skip the theater run.

ratings.plot: Four strangers' paths cross by chance, leading to complex emotional entanglements that challenge their existing relationships and force them to confront uncomfortable truths about love and commitment.

verdict.reason: Lee Chang-dong's first film in a decade demands the theater—his control of ensemble entanglement and moral ambiguity has only sharpened since Burning. The 164-minute runtime is built for patience, not speed, and this is the kind of intimate emotional architecture that collapses on a TV screen.

ratings.plot: Rose, a German widow, hides from Russian soldiers who like to rape women and fights off Polish refugees who will steal everything she has. She gets help when Tadeusz, a former Polish officer, arrives looking to hide from his past.

verdict.reason: A harrowing 90-minute film about survival in post-war chaos that earns its moral weight without sentimentality. Smarzowski's unflinching direction and the confined setting make this a punishing but necessary theatrical experience.

ratings.plot: A criminal on the run hides in a circus and seeks to possess the daughter of the ringmaster at any cost.

verdict.reason: Browning's strangest masterpiece belongs on the big screen, and Lincoln Center's print restores the full grotesque power of a silent film that still shocks. Lon Chaney's performance—playing an armless criminal who manipulates desire itself—is the kind of physical storytelling that only works in a theater.

ratings.plot: In secret conversations on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza are revealed by the people who designed and operated them.

verdict.reason: This is essential testimony about systems of mass killing, told directly by those who built and operated them. The film's power lies in the specificity of rooftop testimony and the willingness of insiders to speak on record about calculated civilian death.

ratings.plot: Thirty-four days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss. From boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim comes YOU CAN SEE EVERYTHING.

verdict.reason: Nathan Fielding and Lance Oppenheim have made something genuinely disorienting about power, performance, and the camera's complicity—a three-hour document that earns its runtime. The film's structural ambition (letting Holmes control her own image while the filmmakers undermine it) is best experienced on the big screen where the manipulation becomes tactile.

ratings.plot: A young Buenos Aires mother finds employment as a sex worker and struggles to live under the same laws that are supposed to protect her.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of a sharp, unsentimental look at survival and state indifference in Buenos Aires. Berneri's direction stays close and observational, letting the material breathe without manipulation.

ratings.plot: Soon after a stranger arrives in a little village, a mysterious sickness starts spreading. A policeman, drawn into the incident, is forced to solve the mystery in order to save his daughter...

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for one of the great horror films of the past decade, a film that demands the big screen and repeated viewings. Na Hong-jin's command of suspense, ambiguity, and visual storytelling across 156 minutes is uncompromising, and Metrograph's presentation gives you the image as intended.

movies.title: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom

ratings.plot: On Halloween Eve at Mossy Bottom Farm, excitement turns to dismay when the clumsy Farmer ruins the pumpkin patch. Shaun tries fixing it with science experiments, but things go wrong when a wild beast appears in the woods.

verdict.reason: Aardman's stop-motion charm and visual invention make this a theatrical event that demands the big screen. The studio's tactile animation and slapstick timing lose their magic on a small device.

ratings.plot: A portrait of genius music composer Ryuichi Sakamoto.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of one of the essential music documentaries of the decade. Schible captures Sakamoto's final creative period with intimate access and formal sophistication that demands a big screen and proper sound.

movies.title: The Taking of Pelham One Two Three

ratings.plot: Four armed men hijack a New York City subway car and demand a ransom for the passengers. The city's police are faced with a conundrum: Even if it's paid, how could they get away?

verdict.reason: See this on 35mm at Metrograph—a masterclass in procedural tension that invented the hostage thriller template and still executes it better than anything made after. Sargent's editing is so precise and propulsive that 104 minutes feels like 60, and the subway car becomes a pressure cooker that never releases.

ratings.plot: A high-strung news producer finds herself in a love triangle between a talented but self-doubting reporter and a charming new anchor, who embodies the growing trivialization of news that she is determined to fight against.

verdict.reason: One of the sharpest films about journalism, ambition, and the cost of principle — see it restored at Metrograph while it plays. Holly Hunter's performance is a masterclass in conveying intelligence and heartbreak through restraint.

ratings.plot: A psychopath tries to forcibly persuade a tennis star to agree to his theory that two strangers can get away with murder by submitting to his plan to kill the other's most-hated person.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's tightest thriller—a masterclass in moral entrapment and manipulation that builds dread through conversation alone. Metrograph is showing a 35mm print of one of cinema's essential films.

ratings.plot: A young African-American man grapples with his identity and sexuality while experiencing the everyday struggles of childhood, adolescence, and burgeoning adulthood.

verdict.reason: A film of rare emotional precision and formal beauty that demands the big screen. Barry Jenkins composes in light and silence, letting long takes and natural sound create intimacy no smaller format can match.

ratings.plot: An executive of a Yokohama shoe company becomes a victim of extortion when his chauffeur's son is kidnapped by mistake and held for ransom.

verdict.reason: One of Kurosawa's sharpest films about class and moral compromise — essential on 35mm at Metrograph. The architectural compositions of Tokyo's vertical city are designed for the theatrical frame, and the second half's procedural intensity builds to a knockout final act.

ratings.plot: Portrait of a middle-class family in Taipei. A man in his forties, his teenage daughter and his eight-year-old son experience life, navigating between remorse, hope and disappointment.

verdict.reason: Three hours of Yang's architectural precision and emotional intelligence—one of cinema's great family portraits. The Metrograph screening honors a filmmaker whose work rarely gets theatrical revival.

ratings.plot: A young couple trying for a baby moves into an aging, ornate apartment building on Central Park West, where they find themselves surrounded by peculiar neighbors.

verdict.reason: This is essential viewing on 35mm at Metrograph, where Polanski's control of apartment geometry and shadow transforms paranoia into lived experience. The restoration reveals details in every frame that casual viewing misses—watch it in the format that makes the space itself a character.

movies.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

ratings.plot: Follows Latif, a devoutly religious hitman, who embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children after his wife dies, confronting forces closing in and beliefs threatening to unravel.

verdict.reason: Bassam Tariq has made a vital film about faith, violence, and fatherhood that demands the theatrical experience. The 35mm print at Angelika Film Center restores the texture and moral weight of every frame.

ratings.plot: Fifteen years after murdering his sister on Halloween night 1963, Michael Myers escapes from a mental hospital and returns to the small town of Haddonfield, Illinois, to kill again.

verdict.reason: One of the foundational horror films ever made—see it on a big screen where Carpenter's compositions and sound design still terrify. The simplicity of the premise and execution is the whole point, and it plays infinitely better in a theater than anywhere else.

ratings.plot: A young woman seeks to break a curse by raising $1000 for psychics in a pre-millennium alternate universe. She navigates the seedy underbelly of Trashtown via scooter, encountering bizarre characters along the way.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming queue and catch this at Anthology while it's there—a genuinely inventive comedy-fantasy with a singular visual voice that demands the big screen. Sriram's command of tone and production design across a scooter-bound odyssey through an alternate 90s underworld justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: This Hong Kong-set crime drama follows the lives of a hitman, hoping to get out of the business, and his elusive female partner.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at peak visual invention deserves the big screen, and this restoration at Metrograph makes it essential. The neon-soaked cinematography and fractured editing demand theatrical immersion.

ratings.plot: A research chemist comes under personal and professional attack when he decides to appear in a 60 Minutes exposé on Big Tobacco.

verdict.reason: Michael Mann's 157-minute corporate thriller is essential on 35mm, where the tense editing and meticulous framing of power dynamics come into full focus. Russell Crowe's performance as a man systematically destroyed for telling the truth remains one of the great portraits of professional conscience in American cinema.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan's first mythic epic demands the 70mm theatrical experience he designed it for. This is a nearly three-hour film engineered for maximum format and you lose the whole point at home.

ratings.plot: After enduring years of malfunctioning products, Wile E. Coyote teams up with a local personal injury attorney to take on ACME, the manufacturer of anything and everything used by the Looney Tunes characters.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming wait and catch this hybrid live-action/animation comedy on the big screen while it's here. Dave Green sustains the gag across feature length by making the lawsuit itself the running joke rather than relying on nostalgia alone.

ratings.plot: At Westerburg High where cliques rule, jocks dominate and all the popular girls are named Heather, it's going to take a Veronica and mysterious new kid to give teen angst a body count.

verdict.reason: One of the sharpest satires of American high school ever made—caustic, funny, and structurally airtight in ways most comedies aren't. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the production design and framing that make Lehmann's staging as precise as the script.

ratings.plot: While a zombie virus breaks out in South Korea, passengers struggle to survive on the train from Seoul to Busan.

verdict.reason: A genuinely propulsive zombie film that uses the train's confined space and forward momentum to generate constant tension. Yeon Sang-ho's control of pacing and character dynamics makes the genre material feel earned rather than obligatory.

ratings.plot: "The Washington Post" reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein uncover the details of the Watergate scandal that leads to President Richard Nixon's resignation.

verdict.reason: One of the essential films about journalism and institutional power—see it on a big screen. Pakula's control of tension and space across 138 minutes is what makes this work, and the Metrograph restoration gives you the clarity that every tracked shot and close-up demands.

ratings.plot: An aging widower arranges a marriage for his only daughter.

verdict.reason: Ozu's final film is essential viewing on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration honors the compositional precision that makes this a masterclass in how much cinema can do with stillness and restraint.

ratings.plot: A modern adaptation of the classic Greek tragedy which falls within a social realism. To the law of men, the young Antigone apposes her own sets of values.

verdict.reason: Deraspe's modern retelling of the Greek tragedy cuts deeper than the source material, turning family loyalty and state power into a collision that feels urgent and alive. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, which gives the social realism texture and grain that streaming will flatten.

ratings.plot: Meeting a stranger in a railway station, a woman is tempted to cheat on her husband.

verdict.reason: One of the greatest films about desire and restraint deserves to be seen on 35mm at Metrograph. Lean's control of mood and Celia Johnson's face—caught between longing and duty—survive only in a theater, on film.

ratings.plot: In 19th century Massachusetts, the March sisters--Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy--on the threshold of womanhood, go through many ups and downs in life and endeavor to make important decisions about their futures.

verdict.reason: Gerwig's adaptation captures the novel's emotional architecture with formal inventiveness that justifies the theatrical experience. The nonlinear structure and sharp editing make this feel like discovery rather than dutiful prestige drama.

ratings.plot: When a nobleman is threatened by a family curse on his newly inherited estate, detective Sherlock Holmes is hired to investigate.

verdict.reason: Terence Fisher's 1959 Hammer version is the definitive screen adaptation of the novel, marrying Gothic atmosphere to detective plotting with rare grace. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings back the color and texture that made Fisher's horror work sing on film.

A rare theatrical screening of Sollas's feminist masterwork demands to be seen large and in company. The 4K restoration reveals the precision of her compositions and the revolutionary clarity of her visual argument about desire and agency.

ratings.plot: Two best friends become stranded on the mystical world of Nakali, where their only escape might cost them their shared lifetime of memories.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming queue and catch this one theatrically—the animation design demands a big screen and the emotional core about friendship and sacrifice lands harder in a theater full of people. The 109-minute runtime moves fast enough to hold attention, and the world-building rewards the full theatrical experience.

ratings.plot: Assigned to a county-mandated drug court program, Cody Parsons embarks on the tenuous journey toward recovery amidst the opioid epidemic in rural Ohio.

verdict.reason: A serious film about addiction and recovery that earns its emotional weight without sentimentality. Adam Meeks directs with a steady hand that lets the performances and the specificity of rural Ohio speak for themselves.

ratings.plot: To satisfy his nagging parents, a gay landlord and a female tenant agree to a marriage of convenience, but his parents arrive to visit and things get out of hand.

verdict.reason: Ang Lee's debut remains a perfect balance of comedy and emotional intelligence about identity and family obligation. Metrograph's 35mm print restores the warm, lived-in textures that made this film feel intimate rather than sitcom-bound.

movies.title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown

ratings.plot: A television actress encounters a variety of eccentric characters after embarking on a journey to discover why her lover abruptly left her.

verdict.reason: Essential Almodóvar at peak invention, vital in 35mm. The 88-minute runtime moves like a perfectly wound toy, and Metrograph's print restores the saturated color palette that makes every frame feel like a poster.

movies.title: The Flavor of Green Tea Over Rice

ratings.plot: A childless middle-aged couple faces a marital crisis.

verdict.reason: One of Ozu's finest films on 35mm at Metrograph is a rare chance to see this restoration on the format it was shot for. The composed domestic scenes and Ozu's pillow shots reward the stillness that only cinema allows.

ratings.plot: Three amateur robbers plan to hold up a Brooklyn bank. A nice, simple robbery: Walk in, take the money, and run. Unfortunately, the supposedly uncomplicated heist suddenly becomes a bizarre nightmare as everything that could go wr...

verdict.reason: One of the essential New York films, a masterwork of tension and character that demands the big screen. IFC Center is showing a 35mm print of Lumet's 1975 classic, the only way to see it done right.

ratings.plot: Haru and Luis love competing in Tokyo's ballroom dance scene, but after tragedy strikes, Haru withdraws into isolation. When friends coax her back to the studio, she develops an infatuation with the new instructor.

verdict.reason: Josef Kubota Wladyka makes films that find genuine emotion in specificity, and a 122-minute comedy-drama about Tokyo's ballroom dance world earning this level of regard suggests real craft. The setting and the focus on how dance becomes a path back from grief gives this genuine theatrical weight.

movies.title: If I Go Will They Miss Me

ratings.plot: A boy sees ghostly figures of other boys in his neighborhood while grappling with his father's distance. These visions uncover hidden connections between them and their shared heritage.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that earns its acclaim through precise observation of grief and inheritance rather than sentiment. Walter Thompson-Hernandez builds the supernatural around a boy's longing for his father with the restraint of someone who understands that the uncanny works best when rooted in real emotional distance.

ratings.plot: A study of the lives and romantic entanglements of various interconnected women.

verdict.reason: Cukor's ensemble masterpiece belongs on the big screen—a rare theatrical revival of one of Hollywood's sharpest comedies about female friendship and betrayal. The all-woman cast and rapid-fire dialogue are built for cinema, not streaming, and Film Forum's 35mm presentation honors the original's visual wit and pristine black-and-white cinematography.

movies.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma

ratings.plot: A director making a slasher sequel becomes obsessed with casting the original film's 'final girl,' leading both women into psychological and sexual chaos.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun's metafictional horror-comedy uses the obsession between director and actress to crack open how desire, ego, and cinema remake each other into something ugly and magnetic. The 35mm print at Village East is the right format for a film this deliberately artificial and visually composed.

ratings.plot: A woman who agrees to a deal to help an old acquaintance. She follows the hero on his adventure and enters dangerous territory where she is then confronted with her own desire.

verdict.reason: Valeska Grisebach's first narrative feature demands a theatrical commitment at nearly three hours, but her control of landscape, tension, and psychological texture justifies the runtime. The film builds moral complexity through patient observation rather than exposition, which only works if you surrender to the screen's scale.

ratings.plot: After earning a licence to kill, secret agent James Bond sets out on his first mission as 007. Bond must defeat a private banker funding terrorists in a high-stakes game of poker at Casino Royale, in Montenegro.

verdict.reason: The best Bond film in decades—a genuine reinvention that ditches gadgetry for visceral action and emotional stakes. Daniel Craig's first outing rewrites the franchise rulebook, and the parkour chase and torture scenes hold their power on the big screen.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: A sharp 71-minute documentary that earns its runtime without padding. Myron Levin's direction stays focused and lets the subject breathe.

ratings.plot: Georges and Anne are an octogenarian couple. They are cultivated, retired music teachers. Their daughter, also a musician, lives in Britain with her family. One day, Anne has a stroke, and the couple's bond of love is severely tes...

verdict.reason: Haneke's most humane film demands the theater and rewards patience with one of cinema's truest portraits of intimacy and decline. Metrograph's 35mm print restores the tender, unsparing compositions that define the work.

ratings.plot: While on a trip to Paris with his fiancée's family, a nostalgic screenwriter finds himself mysteriously going back to the 1920s every day at midnight.

verdict.reason: Allen's most purely enjoyable film in decades—skip it only if you've already seen it twice. Metrograph is showing a 35mm print, which means you get the period cinematography and Paris streetscapes as intended, not compressed on a laptop.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in China II

ratings.plot: Arriving by train in Guangzhou, 1895, the trio fight off White Lotus followers, who want to kill all foreigners and the cute, European dressed 13th Aunt. It's not kung fu master Dr. Wong's (Jet Li) last fight.

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui at peak invention—this is action cinema that uses editing and geography like music, not just spectacle. The DCP at Metrograph is the right way to see a film where every frame earns its place.

ratings.plot: On a remote Scottish isle, siblings Isla and Sandy hunt birds and talk to mythical beings while fighting off outsiders. Their lives change when Daniel, an awkward official, arrives to relocate them.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds real comedy in isolation, strangeness, and the collision between community myth and bureaucratic intrusion. Louis Paxton's command of tone and landscape—mixing deadpan Scottish humor with genuinely surreal moments—rewards full attention on a theater screen.

ratings.plot: The Weight, portrays the life of Jung(Cho Jae-Huyn) who grew up as an orphan and was adopted into a family of only a mother and a son. Jung is now a hunchback man due to scoliosis and is a live-in mortician taking care of corpses ...

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of a quietly devastating South Korean drama that earns its emotional power through restraint and specificity. Jeon Kyu-hwan's direction finds profound dignity in the small gestures of a mortician's daily work, and the film's refusal to sentimentalize makes every moment land harder.

ratings.plot: A 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life.

verdict.reason: Matt Johnson captures the restless intelligence and hunger that made Bourdain magnetic, and the film earns its subject by focusing on the formative summer before the fame. The Provincetown kitchen becomes a crucible for everything Bourdain would later chase: risk, authenticity, and the romance of escape.

ratings.plot: While seeking to cure himself of a curse, young warrior Ashitaka stumbles into a conflict between the people of Iron Town and Princess Mononoke, a girl raised by wolves, who will stop at nothing to prevent the destruction of her h...

verdict.reason: One of the essential animated films ever made, full of visual invention and moral complexity that demands the big screen. Miyazaki's layering of landscape, character, and politics into a single frame is the reason to sit in a theater rather than stream it at home.

ratings.plot: A psychologist is sent to a station orbiting a distant planet in order to discover what has caused the crew to go insane.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for one of cinema's greatest meditations on memory and identity, shot with Tarkovsky's hypnotic command of space and time. Metrograph's DCP restoration honors the film's deliberate pacing and architectural cinematography on a proper screen.

ratings.plot: With his debts mounting and angry collectors closing in, a fast-talking New York City jeweler risks everything in hope of staying afloat and alive.

verdict.reason: The Safdie brothers' nerve and craft demand a dark room and loud speakers—the film's manic editing and anxiety are designed for theatrical immersion. The 35mm print at Metrograph adds texture to the neon chaos.

ratings.plot: An upper-class widow falls in love with a much younger, down-to-earth nurseryman, much to the disapproval of her children and criticism of her country club peers.

verdict.reason: Essential Sirk melodrama that defines the form with visual perfection and emotional complexity. The Technicolor cinematography transforms suburban conformity into a lush prison of mirrors and windows.

ratings.plot: A high-school boy in the early 1970s is given the chance to write a story for Rolling Stone magazine about an up-and-coming rock band as he accompanies them on their concert tour.

verdict.reason: Cameron Crowe's best film about the intoxication of music and fame deserves the big screen now. Metrograph's DCP presentation restores the luminous 70s cinematography that makes every tour bus moment and concert scene sing.

ratings.plot: A man who has struggled personally has conflicts with his upwardly mobile lawyer brother and well to-do fiancee and is reluctantly to be the best man at their wedding.

verdict.reason: Charles Burnett's 1983 masterpiece about class and family fracture deserves the big screen at Film Forum. The film's intimate 16mm cinematography and sharp editing catch every moment of tension between brothers with surgical precision.

ratings.plot: From writer-director Chris Marrs Piliero comes a psychological horror about the weaponization of deepfake technology – and the disintegration of truth in a digital-first culture. One app. One click. One life, ruined or ended. As a single piece of synthetic media metastasizes across feeds, the line between what happened and what was generated stops mattering. The film asks the only question left: if everyone will believe it, does the truth need you to?

verdict.reason: A debut feature that weaponizes deepfake horror into genuine unease about digital collapse and the death of shared reality. Piliero shoots synthetic paranoia with the precision of a thriller, not the fuzzy dread of a cautionary tale, and the 92-minute runtime refuses to overstay its welcome.

ratings.plot: An ostracized fisherwoman commissions the local basketmaker to weave her a husband, but when her wicker creation proves unexpectedly extraordinary, his presence ignites jealousy and upheaval that threatens their quiet village.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that trusts its absurd premise enough to let it breathe—the kind of original fantasy-comedy that belongs on a theater screen, not a laptop. Fischer and Wilson sustain the conceit without winking at it, and the Alamo's crowd-friendly room is the right place to discover something genuinely strange.

ratings.plot: The lives of a motherless boy, who is just starting to get interested in women, and his physically abused friend, who lives in poverty, are mixed with more or less innocent childhood experiences and challenges of a number of child...

verdict.reason: Truffaut's most generous film about childhood deserves to be seen in 35mm at a theater built for it. Metrograph's print captures the luminous, digressive beauty that makes this film feel like memory itself.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in China

ratings.plot: Legendary martial arts hero Wong Fei-Hung fights against foreign forces' plundering of China. When Aunt Yee arrives back from America, Wong Fei-Hung assumes the role of her protector.

verdict.reason: Watch it—Tsui Hark's action grammar has never been sharper, and this 1991 film remains the gold standard for how to film martial arts at speed. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see every whip of the cane and every frame of the editing that made this film legendary.

ratings.plot: A teenager at Rushmore Academy falls for a much older teacher and befriends a middle-aged industrialist. Later, he finds out that his love interest and his friend are having an affair, which prompts him to begin a vendetta.

verdict.reason: Anderson's debut feature is essential theatrical comedy about adolescent obsession and the collision of ego with reality. Metrograph's DCP presentation honors the meticulous production design and color palette that define the film.

ratings.plot: A cyborg assassin from the future attempts to find and kill a young woman who is destined to give birth to a warrior that will lead a resistance to save humankind from extinction.

verdict.reason: Essential on a big screen where Cameron's relentless pacing and practical effects hit hardest. The film's influence on action cinema makes this a theatrical priority over streaming.

ratings.plot: An immigrant Romanian family living in Norway is subject to an investigation and faces the scrutiny of the local judicial system.

verdict.reason: Mungiu's first film in five years is a return to form—go see it on a big screen while it's here. The 146-minute runtime rewards patience, and the performance by the lead actor carries the weight of a family destroyed by bureaucracy.

ratings.plot: A cyborg from the future, identical to the one who failed to kill Sarah Connor, must now protect her ten-year-old son John from an even more advanced and powerful cyborg.

verdict.reason: Cameron's action blueprint still holds—this is essential theatrical spectacle that demands a big screen. The liquid-metal T-1000 effects and practical stunt work remain the standard for how to execute science fiction combat.

ratings.plot: Two death-obsessed sisters, outcasts in their suburban neighborhood, must deal with the tragic consequences when one of them is bitten by a deadly werewolf.

verdict.reason: A smart horror film that uses genre mechanics to say something real about female adolescence and rage. John Fawcett's control of tone—balancing dark comedy with genuine dread—makes this a rare werewolf picture that works as both genre exercise and character study.

ratings.plot: A determined taxi driver in Lagos forms an unexpected bond with a group of free-spirited women, leading her into a world of friendship and self-discovery despite the risks along the way.

verdict.reason: Olive Nwosu brings sharp observation to Lagos street life and female solidarity without sentimentality. The 96-minute runtime and ensemble focus on ordinary women's agency make this a rare theatrical moment worth catching.

ratings.plot: Rescued from abandonment and raised by the King and Queen, Oedipus is still haunted by a prophecy--he'll murder his father and marry his mother.

verdict.reason: Pasolini's operatic reimagining of Sophocles is perverse, profound, and rarely screened—the DCP at Metrograph is your chance to experience one of cinema's strangest confrontations with myth and desire. Do not miss it.

ratings.plot: Two melancholic Hong Kong policemen fall in love: one with a mysterious female underworld figure, the other with a beautiful and ethereal waitress at a late-night restaurant he frequents.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-wai's neon-soaked romance is essential cinema on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation brings the saturated colors and kinetic editing to full life.

ratings.plot: When Jonathan Harker rouses the ire of Count Dracula for accepting a job at the vampire's castle under false pretenses, his friend Dr. Van Helsing pursues the predatory villain.

verdict.reason: Fisher's 1958 Dracula is the definitive Hammer horror film, lean and vicious where others bloat. Metrograph's 35mm print makes the Technicolor blood and shadow sing as intended.

ratings.plot: John works with the PreCrime police which stop crimes before they take place, with the help of three 'PreCogs' who can foresee crimes. Events ensue when John finds himself framed for a future murder.

verdict.reason: Spielberg's best action film holds up as a smart thriller about surveillance and free will, not just a vehicle for Tom Cruise stunts. The Metrograph screening gives you a chance to catch a 2002 film that still looks and moves better than most contemporary blockbusters.

ratings.plot: After his mother's sudden death, Socrates, a 15-year-old living on the margins of São Paulo's coast, must survive on his own while coming to terms with his grief.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of a lean, devastating debut at Metrograph that earns its 71 minutes through precise observation rather than sentiment. Moratto's camera stays close to his protagonist's face and hands, letting grief and survival register in glances and small gestures.

ratings.plot: In 2004, an ad director faces a turbulent Christmas weekend. In 2026, a filmmaker turns her story into a screenplay, blurring the lines between reality, fiction, and the people closest to him.

verdict.reason: Almodóvar at Lincoln Center with a premise about the slippage between life and cinema is essential theatrical viewing. The nested-reality structure and 111-minute runtime demand the focus a theater demands, not the distraction of home viewing.

ratings.plot: A brave girl and her friends must escape a kids television show.

verdict.reason: A horror film that weaponizes children's television aesthetics into genuine dread is rare enough to justify the trip. Casper Kelly's control of tone and image design in a 96-minute package means this lands hard without wearing out its welcome.

ratings.plot: A forgotten Peter Parker lives alone as a full-time Spider-Man until mounting pressure triggers a dangerous change and a powerful new enemy emerges.

verdict.reason: Cretton delivers a genuinely fresh Spider-Man film that treats the character as a burnt-out adult rather than a quipping teenager. The 4DX format at multiple locations amplifies the action sequences, which is exactly where this film earns its theatrical ticket.

ratings.plot: A retelling of the Orpheus and Eurydice myth, set during the time of the Carnaval in Rio de Janeiro.

verdict.reason: The film's color cinematography and Carnaval setting require the 35mm print at Metrograph to sing; it's a sensuous, romantic film that feels authentic to its Brazilian setting in ways no restoration can fully capture at home. Essential repertory.

ratings.plot: When the attempt to kill a professor goes wrong, a series of violent events are triggered which force a taxi driver to run for his life.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin's kinetic crime thriller justifies the 136-minute runtime with sustained tension and formal control rarely seen in the genre. Metrograph's DCP presentation lets you see every detail of the precise action choreography and nighttime Seoul cinematography.

ratings.plot: Isolated from the rest of the world in their countryside mansion, an unhappily married couple engages in a series of increasingly violent role playing games in an effort to heal their relationship.

verdict.reason: Saura's psychological thriller about marital breakdown through ritualized cruelty remains unsettling and formally inventive. The Metrograph restoration makes this 1969 Spanish masterwork visible in full clarity for the first time in decades.

ratings.plot: A tale of nineteenth-century New York high society in which a young lawyer falls in love with a woman separated from her husband, while he is engaged to the woman's cousin.

verdict.reason: Essential Scorsese on the big screen where his camera work and Dante Ferretti's production design create the suffocating world of Gilded Age Manhattan. The film's visual storytelling about repressed desire works best in a theater where every glance and gesture fills the frame.

ratings.plot: Members of a street gang known as the Warriors must fight their way from the Bronx to their home turf on Coney Island when they are falsely accused of assassinating a respected gang leader.

verdict.reason: Walter Hill's street symphony deserves the 35mm restoration at Metrograph, where the cool and the violence sing together. This is why repertory programming exists.

ratings.plot: In 2006, To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen sets out to make television history.

verdict.reason: Lance Oppenheim makes a sharp film about the messy reality behind a TV sensation that defined an era. The 110-minute runtime moves fast, and the subject—how Hansen's crusade became theater—has teeth that justify the theatrical experience.

ratings.plot: Several women enter a science fiction author's life over the course of a few years, after the author has lost the woman he considers his one true love.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's most visually ambitious film demands a theater screen and Metrograph's DCP restoration lets the neon-soaked production design breathe. The 129-minute runtime tests patience, but the payoff is a rare work of sci-fi romance that uses visual style as narrative itself.

ratings.plot: When a machine that allows therapists to enter their patients' dreams is stolen, all hell breaks loose. Only a young female therapist, Paprika, can stop it.

verdict.reason: See this on 35mm at Metrograph—Kon's dream-logic animation demands the clarity and grain of film stock to land its visual chaos. Ninety minutes of pure invention that justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: Feature-length version of the documentary TV series Planet Earth (2006), following the migration paths of four animal families.

verdict.reason: A rare 35mm theatrical screening of a landmark nature documentary that demands the scale of a big screen. Fothergill and Linfield's animal migration sequences are shot for cinema, not television, and the print restoration at Metrograph is worth the trip alone.

ratings.plot: A young girl risks everything to prevent a powerful, multinational company from kidnapping her best friend - a fascinating beast named Okja.

verdict.reason: Bong Joon Ho at his most playful, mixing action spectacle with genuine emotional stakes and sharp corporate satire. Metrograph's DCP projection gives the creature design and production scale the theatrical clarity they demand.

ratings.plot: The discovery of a severed human ear found in a field leads a young man on an investigation related to a beautiful, mysterious nightclub singer and a group of psychopathic criminals who have kidnapped her child.

verdict.reason: Lynch's most accessible nightmare—go see it on a big screen before you die. The image is the point: red velvet, yellow corn, and pure darkness require theatrical space to land.

ratings.plot: An alcoholic man and his two young children barely survive in Taipei. They cross path with a lonely grocery clerk who might help them make a better life.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for Tsai Ming-liang's most restrained and humanist work, a rare theatrical showing of a film that demands the big screen. The 138-minute runtime is built entirely around sustained shots of urban isolation—patience is the price of entry, but the visual language rewards it completely.

ratings.plot: Medea is in Corinth with Jason and their two young sons. King Kreon wants to reward Jason for his exploits: he gives the hand of his daughter, Glauce, to Jason as well as the promise of the throne. In exchange, Medea and the boys ...

verdict.reason: Von Trier's debut is essential early work from a major filmmaker — a brutal, formally audacious reckoning with myth that holds nothing back. The 76-minute runtime is economical and punishing, and Metrograph is the right place to encounter it.

ratings.plot: After being institutionalized in a mental hospital, Su-mi reunites with her sister, Su-yeon, and they return to live at their country home. But strange events plague the house, leading to surprising revelations and a shocking conc...

verdict.reason: Kim Jee-woon's layered psychological horror demands a theater's sound design to land its shifts between dread and revelation. The film's final twist punishes inattention—see it once, properly, on a big screen before the ending spoils itself online.

ratings.plot: A couple take a trip to Argentina but both men find their lives drifting apart in opposite directions.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at his visual peak—worth the trip for a masterwork of color, movement, and heartbreak on the big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph lets you see every saturated frame and tracking shot as intended.

ratings.plot: After her beloved boyfriend's suicide, a mourning supermarket worker and her best friend hit the road in Scotland, but find that grief is something that you can't run away from forever.

verdict.reason: Lynne Ramsay's debut is a restless, formally inventive film about grief that moves like it's being chased. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, which means you get the texture of her handheld camera work and the layered sound design the way she intended.

ratings.plot: A devoted wife is visited by her mother, a successful concert pianist who had little time for her when she was young.

verdict.reason: Bergman at his most direct about the specific cruelty of maternal distance, with Ingrid Bergman and Liv Ullmann delivering performances that need to be experienced in a theater. Metrograph's DCP restoration shows the precise framing and light that Bergman used to make silence louder than dialogue.

ratings.plot: While awaiting execution for murder, Baron Victor Frankenstein tells the story of a creature he built and brought to life - only for it to behave not as he intended.

verdict.reason: Terence Fisher's 1957 film is a lean, visually savage reinvention of the monster myth that holds up as pure cinema. Metrograph's DCP restoration shows off the Technicolor blood and Gothic architecture that made this the template for every mad scientist film since.

ratings.plot: While passing through a vacation resort, a newlywed couple encounters a mysterious, strikingly beautiful countess and her aide.

verdict.reason: See it for one of the most seductive vampire films ever made. Kümel's visual approach treats blood and sexuality as elegant design elements rather than exploitation.

ratings.plot: Five friends head out to rural Texas to visit the grave of a grandfather. On the way they stumble across what appears to be a deserted house, only to discover something sinister within. Something armed with a chainsaw.

verdict.reason: One of the most influential horror films ever made demands to be seen on a big screen where Hooper's relentless pacing and raw craft hit hardest. The 83-minute runtime moves like a sprint, and the Alamo's theatrical presentation lets you feel every frame of its still-shocking viscera.

ratings.plot: Two sloppy actors spend a weekend holiday at an uncle's country cottage.

verdict.reason: One of the funniest British comedies ever made—see it on the big screen where every line lands harder. Metrograph's DCP restoration sharpens the deadpan timing and gives the bleakness of 1980s London the visual weight it deserves.

ratings.plot: In 1921, an innocent Polish immigrant woman is tricked into a life of burlesque and vaudeville until a dazzling magician tries to save her and reunite her with her sister who is being held in the confines of Ellis Island.

verdict.reason: James Gray's greatest film—a baroque moral tragedy about exploitation and redemption shot with obsessive formal precision. Metrograph's DCP restoration restores the painterly color and architectural depth that define Gray's vision of 1920s New York.

ratings.plot: A family heads to an isolated hotel for the winter, where a sinister presence influences the father into violence. At the same time, his psychic son sees horrifying forebodings from both the past and the future.

verdict.reason: Kubrick's formal mastery over a haunted house tale makes this essential theatrical viewing. The geometrical precision of the cinematography and production design demands the size and focus of a theater screen.

ratings.plot: The unenviable life of a government-agency clerk takes a horrific turn with the arrival of a new co-worker who is both his exact physical double and his opposite otherwise--he's a confident, charismatic ladies' man.

verdict.reason: Ayoade's visual control and deadpan precision make this Dostoevsky adaptation a rare theatrical experience worth the trip. The DCP projection at Metrograph showcases the film's deliberately artificial black-and-white cinematography and obsessive production design in ways that streaming cannot match.

ratings.plot: While preparing for her daughter's wedding in Paris, Gloria remembers the ceremony years before in Guinea-Bissau which consecrated her father as an ancestor.

verdict.reason: A rare Alain Gomis film demands the big screen, and three hours exploring memory, lineage, and ritual across two continents is exactly what cinema does best. Lincoln Center's presentation honors the scope of a work that moves between Paris and Guinea-Bissau with the deliberation of ceremony itself.

ratings.plot: The spirits of a deceased couple are harassed by an unbearable family that has moved into their home, and hire a malicious spirit to drive them out.

verdict.reason: Burton's design work and Michael Keaton's manic performance have aged into a masterclass of early MTV-era visual comedy. The 92-minute runtime lets the jokes land without overstaying, and this is the kind of theatrical grotesquerie that demands a big screen.

ratings.plot: On July 27, 1986, Queen performed the largest-ever stadium concert at the Népstadion in Budapest in front of 80,000 ecstatic fans. The concert was part of the famed Magic Tour, which was the last time the band toured with lead singer Freddie Mercury. Now, this original concert film has been beautifully rescanned and remastered in 4K alongside a dynamic new audio mix, featuring many of Queen's favorite tracks – "Bohemian Rhapsody," "Crazy Little Thing Called Love," "I Want To Break Free," and "We Are The Champions." With three years to go before the fall of the Berlin Wall, this was the first Western rock concert performed in a stadium behind the then-Iron Curtain. It was of such significance to the Hungarian authorities and film industry that a group of the country's top film cameramen and technicians were brought together to film it for posterity.

verdict.reason: The 4K restoration of Queen's final tour with Freddie Mercury deserves the big screen and pristine sound. This is a historical document of a breakthrough moment—the first major Western rock concert behind the Iron Curtain—shot by Hungary's best cinematographers and now given the restoration it earned.

ratings.plot: After being kidnapped and imprisoned for fifteen years, Oh Dae-Su is released, only to find that he must track down his captor in five days.

verdict.reason: Park Chan-wook's formal control and the brutality of its revenge narrative demand the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the precision in every frame—the compositions, the color, the violence—exactly as Park intended.

ratings.plot: A rain-soaked couple take refuge in the castle of a transvestite mad scientist from outer space who is about to unveil his greatest creation.

verdict.reason: This is the film that invented the midnight movie experience—see it in a theater where the audience participates, not alone at home. Jim Sharman's direction transforms a low-budget cult oddity into pure theatrical electricity, and that energy only exists in a room full of people shouting back at the screen.

ratings.plot: In 1999, a race of she-aliens, the Kilaaks, brainwash Earth's monsters into attacking major cities, prompting a team of astronauts to stop the invaders while the monsters battle Ghidorah.

verdict.reason: A late-period Toho kaiju film that works as both spectacle and oddball Cold War allegory, best experienced on a big screen where the miniature work and monster choreography shine. Honda and Fukuda's direction keeps the ensemble cast and multiple set pieces in sharp focus, making this the rare franchise entry that justifies the theatrical trip.

ratings.plot: Set high in the mountains, fall comes to an end and a family prepares for the long winter ahead.

verdict.reason: Andrew Haigh at his best—patient, precise, and alive to small gestures that say everything. Lincoln Center is the right place to sit with a 117-minute film about time, family, and the weight of seasons.

ratings.plot: The movie is set in chaotic 1920's China, when warlords fought each other for power while Sun Yat-Sen's underground movement tried to establish a democratic republic. The movie tells the story of three young women and two young me...

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui's 1986 action comedy is a rare theatrical screening of a genuine Hong Kong classic that rewards the big screen. The kinetic staging and inventive action choreography were built for cinema, not streaming.

ratings.plot: Vampire hunter Dr. Van Helsing returns to Transylvania to destroy handsome bloodsucker Baron Meinster, who has designs on a beautiful young schoolteacher.

verdict.reason: Terence Fisher's Hammer vampire film is essential Gothic cinema on 35mm at Metrograph. The restored print transforms the color cinematography and practical horror effects into something that streaming flattens entirely.

ratings.plot: One of the most successful designers in high fashion plans his fall 1994 collection. Follow the behind-the-scenes look at the creative side of fashion.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of the sharpest fashion documentary ever made, capturing Isaac Mizrahi at peak creative fever. Keeve's camera work is so intimate and propulsive that 73 minutes at Film Forum feels like a front-row seat to genius working in real time.

ratings.plot: In the deep south during the 1930s, three escaped convicts search for hidden treasure while a relentless lawman pursues them.

verdict.reason: The Coen Brothers at their most playful, shot through with genuine visual invention and a bluegrass soundtrack that matters. Metrograph's 35mm print restores the deliberately artificial color palette that makes the film's Depression-era pastiche sing.

ratings.plot: A businessman accidentally kills The Metal Fetishist, who gets his revenge by slowly turning the man into a grotesque hybrid of flesh and rusty metal.

verdict.reason: A 67-minute fever dream of practical effects and rhythmic sound design that demands the big screen—skip the home version. Tsukamoto's control of black-and-white image and industrial noise creates a sensory assault that only works in a theater.

ratings.plot: When a mysterious entity possesses a young girl, her mother seeks the help of two Catholic priests to save her life.

verdict.reason: One of the essential horror films — see it on a big screen where Friedkin's control of sound and image still lands like a physical blow. The IFC Center is the right place to experience this restoration.

ratings.plot: An anthology of 5 different cab drivers in 5 American and European cities and their remarkable fares on the same eventful night.

verdict.reason: Jarmusch's deadpan ensemble piece is essential Nineties cinema, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the grainy intimacy that makes five strangers in cabs feel like the only story that matters. The film lives in small moments and precise framing—theatrical projection is the only way to catch what Jarmusch plants in the margins of each frame.

ratings.plot: Presented in a surreal, gory and entirely visual manner, Begotten tells of the death of religion, the abuse of nature by Man and a nihilistic outlook on what life ultimately is.

verdict.reason: A restored print of a landmark avant-garde horror film is rare enough to justify the trip. Merhige's vision of visual nightmare—no dialogue, only image and sound design—demands the theatrical immersion this restoration now provides.

ratings.plot: A young college student arrives in a sleepy Massachusetts town to research witchcraft; during her stay at an eerie inn, she discovers a startling secret about the town and its inhabitants.

verdict.reason: A lean, genuinely creepy British horror film that earns its reputation as a cult classic through atmosphere and a final twist that lands. The 76-minute runtime and stark black-and-white cinematography create dread without padding, and this is the kind of midnight-movie gem that plays better in a room full of strangers.

ratings.plot: After his quest to retrieve the fabled Golden Fleece, Jason returns to Greece with powerful sorceress Medea. However, when the king banishes her, it's only human that Medea plots her furious revenge. Can they escape her wrath?

verdict.reason: Pasolini's radical reinvention of Greek tragedy demands the theater—his visual language transforms myth into ritual and rage. The restored DCP at Metrograph restores the textural power of his composed, hieratic frames.

ratings.plot: A woman discovers the newly resurrected, partially formed, body of her brother-in-law and lover. She starts killing for him to revitalize his body and escape the demonic beings that are pursuing him after he escaped their underworld.

verdict.reason: Clive Barker's original vision remains the definitive entry in the franchise—see it in a theater where the practical effects and sound design hit harder. The Alamo Drafthouse screening offers the theatrical experience this film demands, and its influence on horror cinema makes it essential viewing on the big screen.

ratings.plot: A deadly entity from space crash-lands near a small town and begins consuming everyone in its path. Panic ensues as shady government scientists try to contain the horrific creature.

verdict.reason: Chuck Russell's remake is lean, practical creature horror that knows exactly what it is at 95 minutes. The practical effects hold up better than most 80s sci-fi, and this is the right format to experience the blob's relentless consumption on a big screen.

ratings.plot: Female artists, writers, photographers, designers, and adventurers are settled in Paris between the wars.

verdict.reason: A rare restored screening of essential queer cinema history at Metrograph, documenting the creative lives of lesbian artists and writers who shaped modernism between the wars. The DCP restoration brings archival photographs and firsthand testimony into sharp focus, making this a vital theatrical experience for anyone interested in the hidden genealogy of 20th-century art.

ratings.plot: Con artists plan to fleece an eccentric family using an accomplice who claims to be their long-lost uncle.

verdict.reason: A sharp comedy that works on multiple levels, anchored by Sonnenfeld's visual invention and a cast firing on all cylinders. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the production design's deadpan detail to theatrical clarity.

ratings.plot: In the early twentieth century, a Gorgon takes human form and terrorizes a small European village by turning its citizens to stone.

verdict.reason: Terence Fisher's Hammer Horror has real visual invention and formal control that rewards theatrical viewing. The DCP restoration at Metrograph brings out the color and compositional detail in a film that trades on atmosphere and design over jump scares.

ratings.plot: A streetwise young man becomes a bodyguard to score quick cash. He befriends a disillusioned mercenary determined to begin life anew. They find themselves working together to foil an assassination attempt, but their partnership ca...

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui at peak visual invention deserves the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the kinetic chaos that makes this film sing. The action editing alone justifies the trip.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in China III

ratings.plot: Master Wong and his disciples enroll in the 'Dancing Lion Competition' to stop an assassination plot and to battle an arrogant, deceitful opponent.

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui's action choreography in the third installment is still sharp and inventive even as the narrative loses focus. Metrograph's DCP presentation of this 1993 martial arts spectacle is the right way to catch it on a big screen.

ratings.plot: The Autobots must stop a colossal planet-consuming robot who goes after the Autobot Matrix of Leadership. At the same time, they must defend themselves against an all-out attack from the Decepticons.

verdict.reason: A theatrical milestone that killed off half the toy line and traumatized a generation—this 1986 film earned its cult status through sheer audacity, not polish. The 84-minute runtime moves fast enough to forgive the uneven animation, and seeing Orson Welles voice a planet-eating robot on a big screen is the kind of specific 1980s excess you cannot replicate at home.

ratings.plot: A documentary filmmaker and her fellow Generation X graduates face life after college, looking for work and love in Houston.

verdict.reason: Stiller's directorial debut captures the '90s moment better than any nostalgia factory, and it holds up as genuine filmmaking, not a time capsule. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, which means you get the film stock's grain and color saturation the way it was meant to look.

ratings.plot: A computer hacker is abducted into a digital world and forced to participate in gladiatorial games where his only chance of escape is with the help of a heroic security program.

verdict.reason: A landmark 1982 film about digital worlds deserves to be seen on a big screen, and Metrograph's DCP presentation honors Lisberger's visual invention. The neon geometry and early CGI remain striking in theatrical format, where the scale and color separation matter.

ratings.plot: In 17th-century France, Father Urbain Grandier's protection of the city of Loudun from the corrupt Cardinal Richelieu is undermined by a sexually repressed nun's accusation of witchcraft.

verdict.reason: Ken Russell's most audacious and visually unhinged film demands the big screen, and this restoration on 35mm at IFC Center is the only way to experience its baroque excess as intended. The restoration alone justifies the trip—Russell's baroque compositions of hysteria, sex, and power have never looked sharper.

ratings.plot: Two centuries after her death, a powerful human/alien hybrid clone of Ellen Ripley aids a crew of space pirates in stopping the aliens from reaching Earth.

verdict.reason: Jeunet's visual baroque style transforms a tired franchise premise into something genuinely strange and worth seeing large. The 35mm print at Metrograph is the rare theatrical argument for a film that doesn't hold up nearly as well on smaller screens.

ratings.plot: A recently laid off factory worker kidnaps his former boss' friend's daughter, hoping to use the ransom money to pay for his sister's kidney transplant.

verdict.reason: Park Chan-wook's brutal kidnapping thriller deserves the 35mm print at Metrograph, where the saturated color palette and precise compositions demand the big screen. This is essential for anyone serious about modern genre cinema.

ratings.plot: A group of 12-year-olds form a Universal Monsters fan club called Monster Squad, and have to attempt to save their hometown from Count Dracula and his monsters when they show up for real.

verdict.reason: A genuinely fun genre film that earns its cult status through sharp kid-ensemble chemistry and real affection for Universal monsters. Fred Dekker directs with enough style and humor to justify the 82-minute runtime on a big screen.

ratings.plot: An unscrupulous dealer of rare books finds himself at the heart of a string of paranormal events when he is hired to find the last two copies of a text capable of summoning the devil.

verdict.reason: Polanski's baroque mystery thriller rewards patient viewers who surrender to its labyrinthine plotting and occult atmosphere. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the film's shadowy compositions and makes the baroque production design legible in ways video has never captured.

ratings.plot: An exiled filmmaker finally returns to his home country where former mysteries and afflictions of his early life come back to haunt him once more.

verdict.reason: Angelopoulos's glacial masterpiece demands the 35mm print at Metrograph, where its long takes and compositions reveal depths that small screens erase. Three hours of deliberate, haunted cinema about a director's reckoning with history and exile—essential for anyone serious about cinema.

ratings.plot: A mysterious young drifter who calls herself Nomi Malone hitches a ride to Las Vegas, where she finds work as a stripper and sets about clawing her way to the top of the Vegas showgirls.

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's masterpiece of American excess disguised as exploitation trash. The theatrical experience amplifies both the absurdity and the genuine critique of Vegas capitalism.

ratings.plot: It has been fifteen years since the death of her father, Agamemnon, and Elektra still burns with hatred for Aegisztosz, who conspired with Elektra's mother to kill him.

verdict.reason: Jancsó's formal audacity and political urgency make this a rare chance to see a major Hungarian modernist on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration renders the director's signature long takes and landscape compositions with the clarity they demand.

ratings.plot: Anna, an artist, is obsessed with the invasion of alien doubles bent on total destruction. Her schizophrenia is reflected in the juxtapositions of long movie camera takes with violently edited montages: private with public spaces;...

verdict.reason: Valie Export's 1977 avant-garde masterwork deserves a theater screen and the jolt of her radical montage technique. Metrograph's DCP presentation makes this rare restoration accessible for one of cinema's most uncompromising explorations of paranoia and fractured identity.

ratings.plot: To appease offended gods before going to war, a commander must sacrifice his favorite daughter to them but does so under the pretext of marrying her off.

verdict.reason: Cacoyannis's 1977 adaptation of Euripides deserves the 16mm restoration at Metrograph, a venue built for this kind of classical cinema. The film's stark approach to ancient tragedy plays differently on a big screen than it would anywhere else.

ratings.plot: At the end of the war, Odysseus, the wandering hero, with his companions begins his sail back home to the Mediterranean. The conclusion of his adventure is delayed by many natural obstacles and he takes an internal journey of flee...

verdict.reason: A rare 1989 restoration of Piavoli's visually singular take on the Odyssey's final voyage—pure cinema, no dialogue, shot in natural light across Mediterranean locations. Metrograph's DCP presentation honors the film's painterly compositions and the director's uncompromising formal discipline.

ratings.plot: Three vignettes from three different directors that tell stories of ordinary people during Taiwan's Cold War period.
ratings.director: Hsiao-Hsien Hou, Chuang-Hsiang Tseng, Jen Wan

verdict.reason: A rare screening of early Hou Hsiao-hsien at a repertory house is always worth the trip. The DCP restoration makes these three portraits of Cold War Taiwan clearer than they've likely been since their original release.

ratings.plot: Filmed in New York, story of naive young woman from Hong Kong who goes to New York to study. Street-wise cabbie cousin takes care of her in the big city.

verdict.reason: Mabel Cheung's 1987 New York–set romance is a rarity in the canon, tender and specific about immigrant experience and urban longing. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this the time to see it.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: Ridley Scott's definitive cut belongs on the big screen, and Metrograph's DCP presentation honors the film's visual architecture. The 73-minute runtime is a correction, not a truncation—this is the version Scott always intended.

ratings.plot: A young farmer and his lazy father try to help with the construction of the Dniprohes, but he learns that strength is not enough for a worker and joins the Communist party.

verdict.reason: Dovzhenko's 1932 Soviet film is essential cinema, and Metrograph's 35mm print is the only way to see it as intended. His visual poetry and political commitment do not survive digital compression.

ratings.plot: True-life story of a girl of the streets of Buenos Aires who passed for a boy.

verdict.reason: A rare 1975 Argentine film about gender and survival on Buenos Aires streets deserves a theater seat and restoration attention. Metrograph's DCP presentation makes this obscure Murúa work accessible in the format it was meant for.

ratings.plot: Julian, a middle-aged single doctor, meets his childhood friend Pablo again. The latter is back from Africa and has just married a beautiful young blonde, Elena. Julian falls in love with her and tries to seduce her, but she mocki...

verdict.reason: Saura's control of desire and delusion belongs on 35mm—the image work is too precise for anything smaller. Metrograph's print clarifies the psychological geometry that makes this 1967 thriller hold its shape across decades.

ratings.plot: David Lynch cemented his reputation as an uncompromising visionary with BLUE VELVET, one of the most controversial films of the 1980s, burrowing beneath the surface of idyllic suburban America to reveal a sinister underworld of sex and violence. After stumbling upon a severed human ear, a young college student (Kyle MacLachlan) becomes obsessed with investigating its origins and gets entangled with a nightclub chanteuse (Isabella Rossellini) and her psychopathic lover (Dennis Hopper). A masterfully eerie, depraved psychosexual nightmare and one of the greatest films of the 1980s. “Frank Booth is the role Dennis Hopper was born and chemically mutated to own. Sometimes David Lynch can teeter too far into the absurdity for absurdity's sake, but BLUE VELVET remains perfectly balanced as it dives into the dark, bizarre underbelly of society that lurks just below the surface of suburbia. It is also worth noting that BLUE VELVET, when screened in the first month of operation at the original Alamo, was the movie that inspired our strict no-talking policy.” ( Tim League, Alamo Drafthouse founder)

verdict.reason: Lynch's masterpiece demands the big screen and the communal dark—this is where the film's sickly beauty and ugliness hit hardest. Dennis Hopper's Frank Booth is a performance so feral and unhinged that it needs theater sound to land the full psychotic force.

ratings.plot: One of the most derided movies of the 20th century is also one of its most spectacularly misunderstood. The odd-couple tag team of Dutch provocateur director Paul Verhoeven (ROBOCOP, ELLE) and Sleazoid-Hungarian-American writer Joe Eszterhas (FLASHDANCE, SLIVER) first came together with 1992's BASIC INSTINCT, and everyone, including the financial backers and the producer/distributors of this movie, assumed lightning would strike twice for the duo with 1995's SHOWGIRLS. Universally panned by critics upon its initial release, people found the multi-tap combo of inane dialogue, wild over-acting, and extreme obscenity and grotesquerie to be just too much. Then the "so-bad-it's-good" crowd sunk their hollow claws into the movie, claiming it as one of the "best worst" movies of all time. To be sure, yes, this is a movie in which Saved By the Bell 's Elizabeth Berkley sets fire to her TV-star image by grinding her pelvis on Kyle MacLachlan's lap until he simulates sexual climax while Gina Gershon watches. She shoves chips into her mouth and reminisces about her days of eating and enjoying "puppy chow," between bouts of trying to make it as a Las Vegas showgirl "goddess." The assumption that critics and chuckleheads alike have made are that a) Verhoeven and Eszterhas weren't trying to make something with humor (they were), and b) that the surface story is meant to be taken at face value (it's not). Verhoemie don't play that. SHOWGIRLS is a complicated, satirical masterpiece that tests the audience's limits of empathy and challenges some basic assumptions about American dreams of celebrity, pokes at the artificiality of Hollywood glitz and glamour, and shines a light on the misogyny and dehumanization inherent in the entertainment industry, all while keeping the audiences on their toes as they try to know whether they should laugh, cry, or scratch their heads because there are random interruptions by chimpanzees and the fiercest dancing ever committed to celluloid. (Laird Jimenez)

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's satire of Hollywood misogyny and celebrity worship is sharper and more intentional than its reputation allows, and a theater full of people ready to argue about it is exactly where this film belongs. The Alamo Drafthouse screening gives you permission to engage with the film's deliberate provocation rather than dismiss it as accidental camp.

ratings.plot: Cameron Winter, in December 2025, after a months-long sold-out tour with his band Geese, returned to New York to play a single show at Carnegie Hall. This is the movie. Directed and shot on 35mm and 16mm by Oscar-winning filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson (ONE BATTLE AFTER ANOTHER), the crew includes filmmaker and actor Benny Safdie (THE SMASHING MACHINE) and music producer Ariel Rechtshaid (Grammy winner for albums with Vampire Weekend and Adele). GQ praised Cameron Winter’s show at Carnegie Hall as “staggeringly good,” and Nick Cave said he has "a glorious, emotive voice with brilliant, blistering words, a racked and wondrous thing.” Winter’s solo album Heavy Metal was named one of the best of the year by Pitchfork , Rolling Stone , Paste , and Mojo , and Geese’s last record Getting Killed was named the best album of 2025 by The New Yorker , NME , and Stereogum .

verdict.reason: Paul Thomas Anderson directing a concert film on 35mm and 16mm is event cinema; you will not see this image quality or directorial precision applied to live music anywhere else. The single-theater run at Downtown Brooklyn is a hard stop if you care about how cinema captures performance.
