ratings.plot: Mobilizing the full resources of the Ufa Studios, F.W. Murnau ( Nosferatu , Sunrise ) orchestrated a colossal adaptation of Goethe's FAUST that ranks alongside Fritz Lang's Metropolis as the greatest achievement of the German silent cinema. Gösta Ekman stars as the titular alchemist who, struggling with his faith amidst a devastating plague, is offered the power to cure and the gift of youth...in exchange for his soul. As the diabolical Mephisto, Emil Jannings (The Last Laugh) delivers a performance of operatic scale and intensity, by turns charming, comical, and horrific. This special Kino edition contains the Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau Foundation’s meticulous restoration of the original German version of the film (with unique hand-painted intertitles), as well as a lengthier alternate cut prepared by the Ufa Studios in 1930.

verdict.reason: Murnau's visual command and Jannings's operatic malevolence make this essential silent cinema on the big screen. The Kino restoration preserves hand-painted intertitles and gives you access to both the original German cut and the rare 1930 Ufa version in one screening.

movies.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari w/ Invincible Czars

ratings.plot: It is difficult to imagine precisely what cinema would be without its most influential and memorable titles. THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI in particular stands out as one such notable title in the international canon that in its time and forever thereafter has been heralded as a masterpiece of its craft, the singular model for expressionist, black-and-white filmmaking. A landmark of horror filmmaking, its visual style is often copied or paid homage, and its remarkable twist ending has become all but a modern trope. Its long, haunting shadows and canted, dreamlike production design stay with viewers weeks, months, and years following an initial viewing. The film is credited for introducing the "twist" ending and inspired EDWARD SCISSORHANDS by Tim Burton, THE IMAGINARIUM OF DR. PARNASSUS by Terry Gilliam, and Martin Scorsese's SHUTTER ISLAND, all of which share many striking similarities to CALIGARI. "The first thing everyone notices and best remembers about THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI (1920) is the film's bizarre look. The actors inhabit a jagged landscape of sharp angles and tilted walls and windows, staircases climbing crazy diagonals, trees with spiky leaves, grass that looks like knives. These radical distortions immediately set the film apart from all earlier ones." – Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

verdict.reason: Watch it. A 1920 expressionist landmark that shaped everything that followed, and live music transforms a silent masterpiece into an event.

ratings.plot: In the town of Wisbourg, estate agent Mr. Knock is pleased to receive a commission from Count Orlok to find a house for him. He dispatches his young assistant, Hutter, to Orlok's castle in the far-off Carpathians. He tells Hutter to get him to buy the vacant house just opposite Hutter's own. Hutter arrives at his destination safely and the Count is all too eager to buy the proposed property, especially after he sees a photo of Hutter's pretty young wife Ellen. Hutter soon realizes the evil he's dealing with and is locked away while Orlock makes his way by ship to Wisbourg. As Orlok travels to Wisbourg, plague descends in his wake and the people of Wisbourg begin to sense the coming of evil. Hutter eventually escapes Orlok's castle, determined to return home as quickly as possible, but exhausted and ill, finds himself in hospital. Hutter nonetheless arrives home the same day as Orlok and the townsfolk begin to panic over the increasing number of deaths.

verdict.reason: See this foundational vampire film on the big screen with a live band that earned its reputation by understanding silent cinema's rhythmic hunger. Murnau's visual architecture—shadows as living things, composition as dread—demands theatrical space and the Invincible Czars provide the pulse that transforms viewing into ritual.

ratings.plot: Filmed across three sold-out nights at the 65,000-capacity Foro Sol, RAMMSTEIN – LIVE IN MEXICO CITY captures one of the defining performances of the band's monumental five-year world stadium tour in a spectacular concert film directed by two-time Primetime Emmy® Award winner Paul Dugdale. Spanning 135 concerts and witnessed by 6 million fans around the world, the tour marked a major chapter in Rammstein's career. Two-time GRAMMY® nominees with audiences across the globe, Rammstein have brought German-language rock to major venues around the world – combining colossal sound and live production on a scale entirely their own. Featuring 20 career-spanning songs, the film places audiences at the heart of a show where 20-meter-high flames and towering industrial architecture are matched by moments of genuine connection between the band and the crowd. From November 4, 2026, audiences worldwide can experience RAMMSTEIN – LIVE IN MEXICO CITY in cinematic 4K.

verdict.reason: A stadium concert film shot in 4K across three sold-out nights demands the big screen and the sound system. Paul Dugdale's direction of 20-meter flames and 65,000 fans creates a theatrical experience that evaporates on a TV.

ratings.plot: From two-time Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu, a Norwegian woman and her devout Romanian husband relocate with their five children to a remote, close-knit, coastal town. When allegations of abuse emerge, they are forced to confront a system of judgment that blurs the line between concern and prejudice.

verdict.reason: Mungiu's two Palme d'Or wins make this essential, and his ability to expose moral corruption in tight communities has only sharpened. The 146-minute runtime forces genuine reckoning with complicity and judgment in ways that demand a theater's sustained attention.

ratings.plot: Two race car drivers get caught up in a moonshine operation while competing for titles and women.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this 1966 beach-movie hybrid has not aged into cult territory and plays like a forgotten TV pilot stretched to feature length. The runtime punishes what little charm the moonshine-and-racing premise offers.

ratings.plot: A detective investigating a series of murders discovers that they are similar to the slayings that occur in the new script of a Hollywood screenwriter.

verdict.reason: This obscure 1984 horror-comedy has aged poorly and the premise collapses under its own thin logic. The Alamo Drafthouse screening doesn't rescue a film that depends entirely on novelty that no longer exists.

movies.title: The Ghost in the Invisible Bikini

ratings.plot: A corpse has 24 hours to mastermind a good deed without leaving his crypt, to go "up there" and have his youth restored.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this 1966 AIP relic is a sloppy, mirthless slog dressed up in period novelty. The 82 minutes feel twice as long and the gimmick premise collapses fast.

ratings.plot: In Medival England, a sadistic duke plots to kill off all the heirs to the throne of England so he can claim the title crown for himself.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is inept 1969 schlockhorror with no redemptive craft or historical value. Milligan's direction is flat, the gore is unconvincing, and eighty minutes feels like punishment for showing up.

ratings.plot: Three young girls are mysteriously captured and detained on a remote island, they're forced to become matching mates of the three islander brothers who're raised by their grandmother on the island in isolation from the outside wor...

verdict.reason: Skip it; the premise trades on kidnapping and coercion, and there's no reason to believe the execution justifies the discomfort. No director credit, no format distinction, and a standard multiplex release all signal this is disposable thriller work that will play better nowhere.

ratings.plot: An influencer travels to Copenhagen for a documentary about her online fame, but when an obsessive stalker begins tracking her movements, she must confront the terror and reclaim her power.

verdict.reason: Skip it; a stalker thriller about online fame hits every predictable beat without the craft or insight to justify the premise. Mike Nybroe's direction doesn't unlock anything fresh from the concept, and 95 minutes spent watching an influencer run from a fan feels thin even for a multiplex horror film.

ratings.plot: Vera is a young woman in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia who gets entangled in the WW2 spy network and also in the patriarchal society full of powerful, arrogant men with whom she deals bravely and arrogantly.

verdict.reason: A Metrograph screening of a restoration-quality Yugoslav war film with real craft, but the 130-minute runtime and gap between critical and audience response suggest this plays better for history buffs than general audiences. The DCP presentation at Metrograph is the right venue for seeing this, but don't go expecting crowd momentum.

ratings.plot: A filmmaker applies lessons from a Hallmark movie writing workshop to pitch a documentary about concrete.

verdict.reason: John Wilson's deadpan absurdism works best when you're in the mood for conceptual comedy stretched across 100 minutes. The IFC Center and Nitehawk are the right rooms for this kind of meta documentary, but streaming won't kill the joke if you'd rather see it at home.

ratings.plot: A traveling psychic who helps lost souls cross over encounters a powerful entity at a remote house. While investigating its origins, she uncovers dark secrets and faces a deadly threat from an unexpected source.

verdict.reason: A debut horror film with a solid setup deserves a theatrical look, but 105 minutes is a reasonable commitment for an untested director working in a crowded genre. Dave Boyle's first feature will either justify the hype or feel stretched—best judged in a dark room rather than at home.

ratings.plot: A washed-up New York party promoter is forced to turn his life around when an unexpected visitor arrives.

verdict.reason: Jordan Firstman's directorial debut has uneven execution that doesn't justify the 126-minute runtime, despite moments of genuine comic insight. The film works better as a character study than as a structured narrative, making it worth catching at home rather than committing a full evening to it at Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: Follows a mother, her daughter, and a teenage boy blamed for a tragic death as they travel to Tenerife together, confronting grief, blame, and forgiveness on a family holiday that never happened.

verdict.reason: Wollner's new work has real depth, but two hours of grief excavation on a fabricated holiday tests patience without payoff. The Lincoln Center screening matters only if you're tracking her direction after *The Trouble with Being Born*.

ratings.plot: A worried husband hires a beautiful psychotherapist to nurse his delusional wife and help her deal with the death of their child in a car accident. However, the nurse starts playing mind games. Or is he just being paranoid?

verdict.reason: A deeply fractured film that swings between genuine psychological unease and unintentional camp, saved only by its committed central performances and the venue's archival mission. The 117-minute runtime tests patience, but the ambiguity about who is manipulating whom still lands when it works.

ratings.plot: A notorious prison, an invisible force starts killing inmates brutally, compelling enemy gangs and corrupt guards to work together as they try to survive the mounting bloodshed.

verdict.reason: Joko Anwar's prison-set horror-thriller hybrid has genuine genre craft, but the runtime and tonal shifts demand you're in the right mood for a violent, darkly funny Indonesian import. The Alamo Drafthouse showing honors the theatrical craftsmanship Anwar brings to gore and suspense.

ratings.plot: A daughter unravels her father's dark past after his body, missing for 36 years, is found at a horrific crime scene.

verdict.reason: Jordan Downey has made genuinely unsettling work before, but a 111-minute crime-horror hybrid about paternal secrets needs to earn its runtime, and this one may not. The Alamo Drafthouse is the right venue for a film this dark, but wait for word on whether the pacing justifies the commitment.

ratings.plot: Soon after Thom starts operating as an illegal taxi driver in New York City, Claire hires him to drive her to California after her estranged father suffers a heart attack.

verdict.reason: A charming road-movie setup with real chemistry between leads, but the 97 minutes feel padded and the film never justifies a theatrical trip over streaming. The IFC Center is the right home for it, though—intimate venue, small crowd, no distractions.

ratings.plot: As World War II and the German occupation ends, the Polish resistance and the Soviet forces turn on each other in an attempt to take over leadership in Communist Poland.

Karsten apparently has it settled. However, in this provincial German town, a moment of weakness turns to disaster, disappointment soon fuels anger, justice hides behind hypocrisy, and evil gradually unfolds.

verdict.reason: A sharp dissection of small-town hypocrisy and moral collapse that earns its slow burn, but the 112-minute runtime and deliberate pacing demand full attention on a theater seat rather than half-engaged viewing. Asli Özge's direction rewards patience with precise character work and mounting dread, making Lincoln Center the right venue if you're ready to sit still.

ratings.plot: Jack Skellington, king of Halloween Town, discovers Christmas Town, but his attempts to bring Christmas to his home causes confusion.
A troubled marine seeks to reconcile with the survivors of an Iraqi family he and his unit fired on back in 2003.

verdict.reason: A sincere reckoning with American war guilt that earns its emotional weight, but the runtime tests patience and the moral arc arrives predictably. Reed Van Dyk handles the material without flourish, which works against the film when it reaches for catharsis in its final stretch.

ratings.plot: A family's home becomes the center of paranormal activity that opens a doorway to the "other side." With help, they must cross over to get their daughter back.
Explores what it means to be gay throughout different eras, focusing on "three existences" that are connected through themes of sexuality, desire, pain, and inheritance.

verdict.reason: A 155-minute Spanish musical about queerness across time has real ambition, but the runtime and theatrical format make this a commitment that plays better on a second viewing at home. Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo are working at scale here, which means the film either soars or collapses—either way, you'll know within the first hour.

ratings.plot: A somewhat prim and proper Englishman is hired as the tutor to the son of the Japanese ambassador. His life changes when he and the boy are kidnapped by terrorists for political purposes.

verdict.reason: A 1975 action-adventure with genuine craft and an unusual premise, but the 99-minute runtime and uneven execution make it more of a curious artifact than essential viewing. The Lincoln Center screening offers a chance to see a rare print, which justifies the trip only if you're hunting oddball 70s thrillers.

ratings.plot: Paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren work to help a family terrorized by a dark presence in their farmhouse.

After a harrowing plane crash, a Special Forces officer and his combat dog find themselves stranded deep in the Alaskan wilderness. Together, they are forced into a brutal fight for survival against the elements.

verdict.reason: David Ayer knows how to shoot survival action with real muscle, but a man-and-dog wilderness film lives or dies by whether you buy the bond—and 101 minutes is cutting it close. Catch it in 4DX if you want the Alaskan cold to feel like it's in the theater with you; otherwise, this plays just fine at home.

ratings.plot: A homesick, no-nonsense lounge singer decides to leave New York City to spend some time visiting her two sisters and brother on the West Coast. Eventually she falls in love with a down-and-out ex-jazz pianist.

verdict.reason: Walsh's melodrama has strong atmosphere but lacks the punch of his best work. Lupino's performance elevates material that never quite catches fire.

ratings.plot: In 1940, Henri Marre arrives in Vichy with his self-taught political manuscript Notre Salut, hoping to establish himself in the new regime and publish his work. He seeks to save France from collapse—or perhaps himself.

verdict.reason: A serious period film about collaboration and ambition in Vichy France has real substance, but the 155-minute runtime demands commitment to a morally murky protagonist with no clear dramatic payoff. Emmanuel Marre's directorial voice matters more than the material itself, and Lincoln Center is the right venue if you're in the mood for slow, uncompromising European cinema.

ratings.plot: Macbeth, the Thane of Glamis, receives a prophecy from a trio of witches that one day he will become King of Scotland. Consumed by ambition and spurred to action by his wife, Macbeth murders his king and takes the throne for himself.

verdict.reason: Kurzel's 2015 version is visually striking and brutal, but Shakespeare's language and a relatively young Michael Fassbender sometimes strain against the muddy, visceral approach. Watch for ambition; skip if you want the play to breathe.

ratings.plot: From Focus Features and Working Title comes an irresistible new take on Jane Austen's iconic Sense and Sensibility: a charming, witty, and deeply relatable story of love and sisterhood starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles.

verdict.reason: Georgia Oakley brings fresh energy to Austen, but 131 minutes tests patience for a period romance that works just as well on prestige television. The Alamo Drafthouse is a comfortable venue, not a reason to leave the couch.

ratings.plot: During winter break, two students stay in an all-girls boarding school in the company of a terrifying presence.

verdict.reason: Perkins constructs a genuinely unsettling winter-bound dread, but the 93-minute runtime allows the atmosphere to curdle into repetition before the final twist lands. The film's strength is its mood rather than its plot, which means it works better in isolation than as a communal theater experience.

ratings.plot: Three teens discover that their neighbor's house is really a living, breathing, scary monster.

verdict.reason: Skip it if you've seen it before; the theatrical cut holds up as mid-aughts Zemeckis-style motion-capture fun, but it's a home-viewing film unless Nitehawk's projection quality makes the 91 minutes feel essential. The runtime is merciful and the voice work is competent, but there's nothing about the theatrical experience that justifies the trip over streaming.

ratings.plot: A young beautician, newly arrived in a small Louisiana town, finds work at the local salon, where a small group of women share a close bond of friendship, and welcome her into the fold.

verdict.reason: A crowd-pleaser with real charm and strong ensemble work, but the theatrical cut plays better at home where you can adjust the emotional temperature to suit your mood. Herbert Ross directs with warmth rather than depth, and at 117 minutes the pacing sags between the laugh lines.

ratings.plot: The film chronicles the daredevil stuntman Ken Carter's quest to execute a bold stunt of launching a rocket car across the St. Lawrence River from Canada to the United States in the 1970s, facing absurd challenges along the way.

verdict.reason: Michael Dowse brings absurdist energy to a true story about practical madness, but 99 minutes feels tight for a film about the logistics of launching a rocket car across a river. The premise is outlandish enough to justify the trip if you want something lighter than prestige biography, though standard multiplex venues drain the theatrical kick you'd get from the stunt work.

ratings.plot: A mysterious discovery is made on the outskirts of the remote harbor town. The residents find themselves in a desperate fight for survival against something they have never encountered before.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin has made visceral thrillers before, but this 160-minute survival story feels uneven and overextended for its premise. The runtime tests patience in ways the material doesn't justify.

ratings.plot: An unconventional single mother relocates with her two daughters to a small Massachusetts town in 1963, where a number of events and relationships both challenge and strengthen their familial bonds.

verdict.reason: A minor 1990 comedy with uneven tonal control and a bloated runtime that works better as a small-screen watch. The DCP restoration at Metrograph is clean, but the film itself doesn't demand the theatrical treatment.

ratings.plot: Three secretaries turn the tables on their obnoxious boss.

verdict.reason: A sharp comedy with real bite that holds up better than most workplace films from its era, but the theatrical cut plays better on home video where you can pause for the jokes. Dolly Parton's deadpan delivery is the engine that makes the whole machine work.

ratings.plot: Jean and Joan Holbrooke are two sisters who are so close they speak in unison, love the same man, and have the same dreams. In search of an imaginary land - where true love is possible - they start digging through an entire mounta...

verdict.reason: Solid mid-tier film with enough craft to justify a theater trip, but not urgent. Lincoln Center's programming weight carries more of the recommendation than the film itself.

ratings.plot: A young man struggles with his desire to study art when his family thinks he's headed for premedical studies. Conflicts between Filipino traditions and expectations vs. personal dreams in the contemporary world erupt at his sister...

verdict.reason: A sharp-eyed debut about generational collision in a Filipino-American family that works best if you're in the mood for intimate character drama over plot momentum. The 88-minute runtime and ensemble cast keep things moving, but this is a film that rewards patience with specificity rather than broad appeal.

ratings.plot: A bullied teenage boy is devastated after the death of his heavy metal idol, Sammi Curr. But as Halloween night approaches, he discovers that he may be the only one who can stop Sammi from making a Satanic comeback from beyond the...

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're hunting for obscure 80s horror-comedy trash or want to see a heavy metal demon possession film on a big screen. The Alamo Drafthouse programming suggests this is a midnight movie, not a serious theatrical experience, and the film's reputation rests entirely on novelty and nostalgia.

ratings.plot: The life and death of "Dracula" writer Bram Stoker is discussed, as well as the themes of the novel and several film adaptations of "Dracula," and the cultural impact of the work. While critics of the time were not receptive to th...
Four college girls hold up a restaurant in order to fund their spring break vacation. While partying, drinking, and taking drugs, they are arrested, only to be bailed out by a drug and arms dealer.

verdict.reason: Korine's maximalist visual style and James Franco's performance have aged better than the film's shock-value premise, but the 94 minutes still feel self-impressed rather than revelatory. See it at IFC if you're curious about a mid-period Korine work, but streaming captures the neon aesthetic just fine.

ratings.plot: A chronicle of the tragic love affair between American poet Elizabeth Bishop and Brazilian architect Lota de Macedo Soares.

verdict.reason: This is worth seeing if you're drawn to the specificity of Bishop and Lota's relationship, but the film doesn't quite justify its two-hour runtime. Barreto's direction is workmanlike rather than revelatory, and the emotional stakes flatten before the end.

ratings.plot: A New York City architect becomes a one-man vigilante squad after his wife is murdered by street punks. In self-defense, the vengeful man kills muggers on the mean streets after dark.
Years after her Hollywood breakthrough, a talented actress whose career has stalled fights for her second act.

verdict.reason: Chris Rock's directorial debut has real moments but never quite commits to either comedy or drama, making it work best as a mid-week streaming choice. The lead performance carries genuine vulnerability, but the 103-minute runtime drags in the middle act when the script runs out of things to say.

ratings.plot: With the help of a smooth talking tomcat, a family of Parisian felines set to inherit a fortune from their owner try to make it back home after a jealous butler kidnaps them and leaves them in the country.

verdict.reason: A minor Disney entry that works best as a comfort watch at home, but the 35mm print at Metrograph makes it worth catching if you're already in the neighborhood. The restoration lifts what is otherwise a slight, forgettable film into something that justifies a theater seat.

ratings.plot: The hit musical based on the life of Eva Perón (Evita Duarte), a B-picture Argentinian actress who eventually became the wife of Argentinian president Juan Domingo Perón, and the most beloved and hated woman in Argentina.

verdict.reason: The Alan Parker musical lands better on a big screen than at home, but the film's theatrical ambition often outpaces its execution. Metrograph's 35mm print restores the sweeping production design that justifies the trip, though the runtime tests patience and Madonna's performance divides viewers.

ratings.plot: When a frustrated playwright/middle school theater teacher finds out his ex-girlfriend has started dating his nemesis, the school's principal, he decides to ruin the principal's chances of winning the Blue Ribbon of Academic Excel...

verdict.reason: Skip it if you need a sharp script, but the 87-minute runtime and Bonilla's debut energy make this worth a weeknight gamble if you like workplace comedies that swing for the fences. The premise leans on a tired love-triangle setup, but there's real potential in a teacher using theater sabotage as his weapon.

ratings.plot: A grieving father enacts his long-awaited revenge against a ruthless gang on Christmas Eve.

verdict.reason: John Woo's first English-language film in years has genuine craft moments, but the execution is uneven and the premise wears thin before the final act. The Lincoln Center booking is respectable, but this is a minor entry from a major director—worth catching only if you're committed to tracking his recent work.

ratings.plot: A young girl new to a Catholic school befriends a coven of witches whom the other students either shun or fear. But when a powerful invocation goes wrong, the consequences could endanger their lives.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're in the mood for '90s goth camp that hasn't aged well outside of nostalgia. The execution is uneven and it plays better as a streaming rewatch than a theater commitment.

ratings.plot: A designer makes a grievous mistake when he rejects the friendship of a borderline cable guy.

verdict.reason: Skip the trip unless you want to revisit a '90s Carrey outlier that swings wildly between dark comedy and sincere creepiness. Stiller's direction punishes comfort in ways that feel intentional, not accidental, but the film demands the right mood and a big screen doesn't add much.

ratings.plot: A young sheriff's deputy finds himself in the crosshairs of dangerous criminals when the dead body he is assigned to keep an eye on disappears from a crime scene.
Directionless teenager Susanna is rushed to Claymoore, a mental institution, after a supposed suicide attempt. There she befriends a group of troubled women who deeply influence her life.

verdict.reason: Angelina Jolie's performance still carries the film, but the direction is uneven and the script sanitizes Susanna Kaysen's book. The 35mm print at Metrograph makes it worth seeing on a big screen if you're willing to accept that this is a glossy studio take on mental illness, not the real thing.

ratings.plot: Kirsty is brought to an institution after the horrible events of Hellraiser (1987), where the occult-obsessive head doctor resurrects Julia and unleashes the Cenobites and their demonic underworld.

verdict.reason: The sequel trades Barker's vision for studio chaos, but Clive's production design and the Labyrinth sequences still deliver visual invention worth seeing on a theater screen. The 97-minute runtime keeps it brisk enough that the tonal whiplash doesn't kill momentum entirely.

ratings.plot: The most powerful man in the world embarks on a frantic mission to prove he is humanity's savior before the disaster he's unleashed destroys everything.

verdict.reason: Iñárritu's satirical swing at power and catastrophe has ambition, but the execution is uneven and the runtime tests patience without payoff. See it in IMAX if the scope interests you, otherwise wait for streaming.

ratings.plot: In April 1964, more than twenty years after the Nazis won World War II, S.S. officer Xavier March uncovers a plot to eliminate the attendees of the Wannsee Conference so that Germany can establish better relations with the U.S.

verdict.reason: A fumbled alternate-history thriller that wastes its premise, but the 1994 HBO production has enough production design and Rutger Hauer's weary performance to justify a single viewing at Lincoln Center if you're committed to exploring '90s speculative television. The film's earnest mid-budget craft—swallowing the clumsy narrative—holds up better on a theater screen than it would on a small one.

ratings.plot: A classic tale about bitter relationships between a frivolous girl and a soldier is adapted for the post-World War II time.

verdict.reason: Clouzot's adaptation has genuine power but arrives uneven and padded at 100 minutes. The Film at Lincoln Center restoration makes this the only way to see it properly on a big screen, and the post-war Paris setting carries real historical weight if you're willing to sit with the film's tonal shifts.

ratings.plot: Lowen Ashleigh gets hired by Jeremy Crawford to ghostwrite novels for his bestselling author wife Verity, who's unable to finish after an accident. Lowen uncovers Verity's disturbing truths while residing at the Crawfords' home to...

verdict.reason: Michael Showalter has a mixed track record with psychological thrillers, and this adaptation hinges entirely on whether the twists land without feeling contrived. The 4DX and RPX options at major chains suggest the studio is banking on spectacle over substance, which is rarely a good sign for a mystery that needs your full attention.

movies.title: KAMA SUTRA: A TALE OF LOVE

ratings.plot: Two female friends become sexual rivals at maturity.

verdict.reason: Mira Nair's visual command and the 35mm print at Anthology make this worth seeing if you're tracking her work across decades, but the film's dramatic instability and uneven pacing mean it plays better as a repertory experience than as a night out. The cinematography justifies the theater.

ratings.plot: A worldwide epidemic encourages a biotech company to launch an organ-financing program similar in nature to a standard car loan. The repossession clause is a killer, however.

verdict.reason: Skip the multiplexes, but catch it at Alamo Drafthouse if you're in the mood for midnight-movie chaos and don't mind sitting through an uneven pitch. Bousman swings wildly between genuine visual invention and tonal whiplash, but the opera-horror-splatter hybrid commitment is rare enough to warrant one viewing in a room built for cult movies.

ratings.plot: A young soprano becomes the obsession of a disfigured and murderous musical genius who lives beneath the Paris Opéra House.
On vacation in Thailand, Richard sets out for an island rumored to be a solitary beach paradise.

verdict.reason: Boyle's visual ambition salvages a thin premise, but the film indulges its own hype and outstays its welcome. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the digital palette that defined late-90s blockbuster excess, which is worth seeing once on a large screen.

ratings.plot: Dr Marrow enlists Theo, Luke and Nell for a study of sleep disorders at the Hill House. As soon as the terrifying truth about the mansion is revealed, everyone is found fighting for their lives.
Nicolas, the eldest son of a wealthy family, works far from his home environment as a window washer and dishwasher in a bistro. He does not notice at all the baseness of his new relationships.

verdict.reason: Iosseliani's gentle comedies reward patience, but this 1999 film sits between his strongest work and risks feeling slight on a single viewing. The Metrograph DCP gives the provincial French settings clarity, though the 118-minute runtime and episodic structure demand the right mood.

movies.title: Ghost in the Shell: 30th Anniversary Remaster

ratings.plot: Judith is a maverick reporter who is also seeking a satisfying relationship with various men. She finds corruption and power-games everywhere.

verdict.reason: A rare Valie Export screening at Metrograph rewards patience with her distinctive formal intelligence, but the film's 1985 dating and fragmented structure demand active viewing rather than passive consumption. The DCP restoration preserves Export's precise visual language, though the 86 minutes feel deliberately constructed to resist easy engagement.

movies.title: Art Cinema for Tots: How to Play a Film
Bread Day preceded by The Train Stop

ratings.plot: Elisa hasn't seen her father Luis in nine years, but she receives a telegram from her sister at a time of crisis in their marriage informing her that her father is sick and decides to travel to Madrid to visit Luis for his birthday.

verdict.reason: Saura's intimate chamber drama rewards patient viewers but demands commitment to two hours of slow-burn family reckoning. The Metrograph screening preserves a restoration of a minor work from a major director—worth seeking if you're already in the neighborhood.

ratings.plot: A wimpy, incompetent bank clerk decides to become a pro wrestler.

verdict.reason: Kim Jee-woon's comic wrestling film is a charming oddity at Metrograph, but it's a minor work that gains little from theatrical scale. Worth seeing if you're already catching something else at the venue.

ratings.plot: Prometheus engages in repeated scenes of bisexuality in this independent feature from the New York underground.

verdict.reason: Markopoulos's 1967 underground film is formally radical and historically significant, but 16mm projection at Metrograph demands patience and an appetite for structuralist cinema. Go if you're prepared for experimental rhythm; otherwise stream it.

movies.title: Trains Children & Dreams: A Shorts Program

ratings.plot: "Virgina" tells a tale from the end of the 19th century. It took place in a isolated village near the Adriatic Sea. Because of the extreme patriarchal culture there is a superstition that families without male heirs are cursed. Wh...

verdict.reason: A rare 1991 Balkan drama about patriarchal superstition deserves screening, but the film's reputation suggests uneven execution and a 101-minute runtime that tests patience. Metrograph's DCP presentation is clean, though the material itself is the real draw for cinema historians tracking Yugoslav cinema.

ratings.plot: A mysterious young girl wanders a desolate, otherworldly landscape, carrying a large egg.
Siblings Sara and Sean Porter return to their rural childhood home on the 26th anniversary of their Mother's infamous UFO sighting.

verdict.reason: A genuine rarity with an intriguing premise, but the 79-minute runtime and thin plot description suggest this is a modest indie drama that may not justify the trip unless you're committed to discovering obscure work. Film Forum's theatrical platform elevates it, but without knowing the execution, this is a home screening candidate if it reaches streaming.

ratings.plot: Teen Isabel's attraction to Dr. Palanca at her country club job turns dark as she uncovers violence beneath the club's facade and discovers their disturbing connection from the past.

verdict.reason: Rafael Manuel's film has genuine unsettling power, but the runtime and tonal shifts demand patience on a big screen rather than at home. Film Forum's single-theater run means the screening window is narrow and the audience self-selected.

ratings.plot: The disappearance of the leading actor from the film's set worries its director Andrzej. He embarks on a journey to look out for the actor with a young actor and missing actor's wife and mistress.
A provocative examination of celebrity haters, public vitriol, and the toxic price of fame.

verdict.reason: Rory Kennedy's documentary work has substance, but this arrives as a live-trial event that may feel dated the moment the verdict lands. The theatrical window matters less than timing; stream it when the legal outcome is final and you can sit with the whole story.

ratings.plot: A man takes his sick mother and nine family members on a single-day temple pilgrimage after his boss predicts she may die soon.

verdict.reason: A debut feature from a Thai filmmaker working in an intimate mode—worth seeing if you trust Lincoln Center's curatorial judgment on emerging international voices. The single-day structure and family ensemble suggest a quiet, character-driven film that may play better on a second viewing at home.

ratings.plot: In October 1980, twenty environmental experts convene at a Florida hotel to draft a congressional statement on carbon dioxide emissions, but struggle to agree on the wording.

verdict.reason: Tom McCarthy has made sharp ensemble comedies before, but a two-hour film about bureaucratic wordsmithing lives or dies on whether the script finds real absurdity in the process. The premise promises good material—a room full of experts paralyzed by consensus—but McCarthy's restraint sometimes undercuts the satirical potential.

verdict.reason: A short sci-fi film screened at Lincoln Center has enough venue credibility to justify the trip if you're already in the area, but the runtime and director are unknown, making it impossible to assess theatrical urgency. Without basic production information, treat this as a programming gamble rather than a must-see.

ratings.plot: A young theatre director Petr Dresler accepts an offer to direct the show "Last Train to Sussex Has Gone" in a great Prague theatre. The play is a modern piece of art from a famous author ...

verdict.reason: A Czech backstage comedy about theatrical ambition has real charm, but it's a minor regional film playing a single venue with no restoration or special occasion attached. Watch it if you're at Lincoln Center for something else and have time to kill; otherwise, this one doesn't justify the trip.

verdict.reason: A three-hour opera film demands commitment, but Metge's take on Mozart's comedy has real wit if you're in the mood for theatrical excess. The Lincoln Center screening gives you the proper scale, though streaming at home won't punish you much.

ratings.plot: Annie struggles to to clear his bachelor's degree with one final hurdle-The Thesis. It's his final attempt to clear it. Can he?

verdict.reason: A rare 1989 Indian comedy from Pradip Krishen deserves the Lincoln Center screening, but the thin premise and two-hour runtime demand patience if you're unfamiliar with the film's reputation. The theatrical venue and print quality justify a trip only if you're hunting for overlooked work from this era and director.

verdict.reason: A 1912 Italian film at Lincoln Center is historically significant but requires patience with silent-era pacing and image degradation. See it if you are committed to early cinema archaeology; skip it if you need theatrical polish.

ratings.plot: Richard Wagner's last opera has remained controversial since its first performance for its unique, and, for some, unsavory blending of religious and erotic themes and imagery. Based on one of the medieval epic romances of King Art...

verdict.reason: Syberberg's four-hour operatic vision is uncompromising and visually baroque, but demands absolute commitment and tolerance for his deliberately confrontational staging of Wagner's final work. The theatrical experience is singular, though patience and appetite for avant-garde opera aesthetics are prerequisites.

ratings.plot: The story revolves around the incidents following the death of a young Naxalite, upon whose death his friends travel to the village where his mother lives to inform her of the death of her only son.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of an obscure 1986 Indian political drama about grief and state violence—worth seeing if you seek out work beyond the festival circuit. Lincoln Center's archive programming makes this the only accessible way to experience John Abraham's direction on the subject of Naxalite resistance and maternal loss.

The Alamo Drafthouse screening is built for a crowd that will eat the melodrama alive, which is half the appeal and half the reason to wait for home viewing.

ratings.plot: Jay Gardiner is having a whale of a bad day. While diving off the California coast to recover his late father’s remains, he gets swallowed whole by an 80-foot sperm whale and has one hour of oxygen to escape. Austin Abrams, currently having a major moment after starring in Zach Cregger’s RESIDENT EVIL, leads this adaptation of Daniel Kraus’ bestselling novel. Yes, it’s a movie where a guy gets swallowed by a whale, but it’s also a tense and even moving tale of survival, grief, and family. Dive in on the big screen.

Rise Azumino is a university student who feels lost in her life. One day, guided by an invitation letter left behind by her late grandmother, she enters “Wonderland”. The Queen of Hearts, the Mad Hatter, Cheshire Cat…the residents of Wonderland appear before Rise one after another and crazy commotion ensues! verdict.reason: Skip it unless you have a specific appetite for anime riffs on Carroll. This is a loose, contemporary framing device bolted onto Wonderland rather than a fresh take on the source material, and the 97 minutes suggest rushed execution.

ratings.plot: Jane Austen gets another trip to the big screen, with Daisy Edgar-Jones (TWISTERS) and Esmé Creed-Miles (HANNA) leading a fresh take on the Dashwood sisters and their tangled romantic lives, directed by Georgia Oakley (BLUE JEAN). It’s Austen by way of a modern romantic comedy, where money is tight, feelings are tighter, and “I greatly esteem him” is Regency-speak for “I have it bad for this man.” Sisterly solidarity, social maneuvering, and romantic complications are all on the menu.

verdict.reason: Georgia Oakley brings a sharp directorial eye to Austen, and the cast chemistry between Edgar-Jones and Creed-Miles has real spark, but 132 minutes of romantic complications plays better on a smaller screen at home. The Alamo Drafthouse food-and-drink setup works against the delicate social comedy at the heart of this one.

ratings.plot: Bela, an 8-year-old girl living in a home with marital problems, confronts a sinister entity which comes out of her closet. The presence, whom she calls "Other Mommy," becomes increasingly threatening to her and her family.

verdict.reason: Rob Savage has made lean, inventive horror before, and a 93-minute creature feature about a child's terror is at least focused, but an unknown entity-in-the-closet premise needs sharp direction to avoid familiar scares. The Alamo Drafthouse chain suggests this is built for a genre audience that will get more out of the theatrical sound design than a solo viewing at home.

ratings.plot: At Chester’s cottage, good behavior earns karaoke. Getting answers is a little more complicated. After a mysterious apocalyptic(ish) attack leaves them bloodied, disoriented, and unable to speak, Liam (Joey Bader) and Mel (Kaylee McGregor) take refuge in the English countryside. Their oddball host, Chester (Oliver Woolf), feeds them, helps them recover, and introduces a system of rewards: behave yourself, earn “nifties,” cash them in for hot-tub time and dance parties. Beyond the cottage, things are less nifty. But within it, a makeshift family is taking shape. While Liam embraces their new life, Mel grows increasingly curious about the world Chester insists is too dangerous to enter… In their feature debut, directors Scott Tinkham and Michael Woloson mix deadpan comedy, sibling rivalry, and creeping unease in a coming-of-age story about people who have to grow up all over again. Winner of the Special Jury Prize at the 2026 Manchester Film Festival and the Narrative Feature Audience Award at Dances With Films LA 2026, this has the sort of sensibilities that fans of Yorgos Lanthimos and Ben Wheatley will adore… and it’s a natural fit as an Alamo Exclusive.

verdict.reason: Feature debut directors mixing deadpan comedy with creeping dread shows real promise, but an 88-minute runtime and premise built on mystery mean this lands harder with the right mood than as a guaranteed night out. The Alamo Drafthouse exclusivity and festival wins suggest this is worth catching in a theater with people who'll get it, but streaming will likely be fine if you're not committed to the vibe.

ratings.plot: After a seven-year hiatus following the devastating loss of their beloved bandmate Chester Bennington, Linkin Park's remaining members struggle to find their way forward. Their shared history and enduring friendship, combined with the fresh perspective of two new band members, spark a renewed creative energy that leads them on a transformative journey of artistic reinvention. Following the band from intimate 2022 studio sessions through their explosive From Zero album release and concert in São Paulo, the film UNSHATTER weaves together rare vault footage, electrifying performances from sold-out shows, and candid interviews with band members and fans – capturing the raw, honest story of what it means to start over.

verdict.reason: A competent band documentary that works if you're invested in their story, but it's a standard concert-and-studio-sessions film without the directorial vision that lifts music docs into the essential category. The 4DX and ScreenX options at Village East and Regal locations feel gimmicky for what is primarily talking heads and performance footage.

ratings.plot: 40 YEARS OF FUCKIN' UP is SPINAL TAP, but real. It's a film about the infamous, fairly unfamous, and beloved punk rock band NOFX. This is the unbelievable story about how a group of untalented, drug-addicted teenage punks somehow became the most successful independent band in history – and they did it haphazardly, entirely on their own.

verdict.reason: A chaotic, fun ride for NOFX devotees and punk history buffs, but the two-hour-plus runtime tests even true believers. The Alamo's beer-and-heckle atmosphere is the right venue for this kind of controlled mess, which matters more than the film itself.

ratings.plot: Street Fighters Ryu and Ken reunite when Chun-Li recruits them for the World Warrior Tournament. As they face a hidden conspiracy, they must confront each other and their past-or face destruction.

verdict.reason: A live-action fighting game adaptation has never landed, and this one carries real risk despite Kitao Sakurai's pedigree as a character action director. The two-hour runtime and tournament structure suggest theatrical ambition, but the premise hinges entirely on whether Sakurai can make hand-to-hand combat feel earned rather than choreographed spectacle.

ratings.plot: Follows Frances Haugen, a young Facebook engineer, who enlisted the help of Jeff Horwitz, a Wall Street Journal reporter, to blow the whistle on the social network's most guarded secrets.

verdict.reason: Sorkin's playbook of rapid-fire dialogue and structural precision fits the whistleblower-meets-reporter story, but the stakes feel domesticated at 112 minutes when the material demands either sweeping scope or intimate focus. ratings.plot: Presented in Spanish with English subtitles "A rousing maximalist slice of magic" – A.V. Club From Cannes-winning directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi – popularly known as Los Javis – LA BOLA NEGRA follows three generations of men across pivotal moments in Spanish history, bound by pain, desire, and love. Carlos (Milo Quifes) longs to belong in a fractured Spain. Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) finds connection across enemy lines. verdict.reason: Three hours is a steep ask for a debut feature, even one from accomplished directors, but the Spanish-language scope and generational ambition reward patience if you're in the mood for formally ambitious work. Catch it at Alamo Drafthouse with an audience if you trust Los Javis' track record in television to translate to film.

ratings.plot: Imagine that a local cable station was invaded by otherdimensional creatures at the stroke of midnight. That's Video Vortex. Each month, this series presents a mystery transmission that's culled from the outer limits of home video history – from essential underground films to surreal docs, from tokusatsu battle-parties to outsider experiments. So warm up the cathode tubes, dim the lights, and let your senses intermingle with the glow.

verdict.reason: Alamo Drafthouse's curated grab bag of obscure home video ephemera is a fun gamble for adventurous viewers, but the quality and thematic coherence are unknown by design. Show up if you trust the curation; skip if you need a guarantee.

ratings.plot: Celebrate Doctor Who Day with an exclusive big-screen event marking 20 years of the Tenth Doctor and Rose Tyler. For the first time ever in cinemas, the acclaimed two-part adventure The Impossible Planet and The Satan Pit has been specially re-edited into a single movie-length presentation, created exclusively for theatrical audiences. Join the Doctor (David Tennant) and Rose (Billie Piper) as they travel to Sanctuary Base 6, a remote outpost perched on a planet orbiting a black hole. When an ancient force awakens beneath the surface, the crew find themselves trapped in a battle against an evil older than time itself. This special Doctor Who Day screening also includes exclusive bonus material, featuring previously unseen content and a brand-new interview with a special guest, reflecting on the making of one of the most celebrated stories of the modern era – from encounters with the Ood to facing the terrifying Beast, alongside behind-the-scenes memories from the set.

verdict.reason: A theatrical recut of a beloved two-part episode with exclusive bonus material makes for a strong event, but the 115-minute runtime and limited venue mean this plays better as a fan pilgrimage than a casual night out. Tennant and Piper's chemistry and the Satan Pit creature design are genuinely worth the big screen if you're already committed to the Doctor Who calendar.

movies.title: Ozzy & Black Sabbath: Back to the Beginning

ratings.plot: OZZY & BLACK SABBATH: BACK TO THE BEGINNING documents a landmark moment in music history: Ozzy Osbourne’s historic final farewell performance for his fans at Villa Park stadium in his Birmingham hometown, captured just 17 days before his untimely passing. The film highlights the historic day with performances from Ozzy, Black Sabbath, and some of the most influential names in rock, along with personal reflections from the superstar musicians they inspired and a behind-the-scenes look at the day itself. This is an historic and intimate farewell to Ozzy and the band that changed music forever.

verdict.reason: A competent concert document of genuine historical weight, but the 147-minute runtime and single-theater NYC availability make this more of a pilgrimage than a casual night out. Stream it at home unless you need to witness Ozzy's final bow on the biggest screen possible.

ratings.plot: A gifted cellist, Alex Serian (Pedro Pascal), returns home to Los Angeles after 20 years on the road. Music, which has been the constant, all-consuming river of his life, begins to carry Alex on an adventure that will change him forever.

verdict.reason: Pedro Pascal carries a film about a musician's midlife reckoning with genuine depth, but the two-hour runtime and introspective pace work better on a smaller screen than in a theater seat.
